Hacker News.article_text: Open-source AI agent framework for PHP. Tools, memory, security guards and a ReAct loop built in. Works with Laravel, Symfony, WordPress, Drupal, Magento, Joomla, OpenCart, PrestaShop. Any LLM prov... Tools, memory, security, and a ReAct loop, already built. Zero framework dependencies in core. Any LLM provider. One env var, one builder, one send() . The builder checks ANTHROPIC_API_KEY , then OPENAI_API_KEY , GROQ_API_KEY , GEMINI_API_KEY , MISTRAL_API_KEY , DEEPSEEK_API_KEY , OLLAMA_HOST , in that order, and uses whichever it finds first. No YAML, no agent framework to learn, no vendor lock-in. An agent without tools can only talk. Register the ones your application needs and it starts doing real work: The agent decides which tools to call and in what order, running a ReAct loop (reason, act, observe, repeat) until it has an answer or hits the iteration cap. This works identically whether the tools touch your shell, your database, your HTTP APIs, or your codebase. Every "AI in PHP" tutorial ends the same way: an HTTP client bolted onto a provider API, a hand-rolled tool-call loop, and a prayer that the prompt holds up in production. A generic LLM SDK gives you the API client. phpClaw gives you the agent runtime around it: the loop, the guards, the memory, the framework wiring, already assembled. Not trying to be everything. phpClaw isn't a RAG framework: there are no embeddings or vector stores. It's built to give an LLM tools, memory and security controls against your real application, and to chain those agents into pipelines and graphs when one call isn't enough. Agent runtime. A ReAct loop with a hard iteration cap ( max_iterations , default 20), pluggable tools, pluggable memory, and skills the model loads on demand through the load_skill tool, all running inside a single reasoning cycle. Pipelines and graphs. Pipeline chains steps (prompt template, agent, structured output, your own callables) with retry and fallback. Graph runs nodes that loop, branch, pause for a human, resume in another process, and fan out to branches that run inline or are drained by workers from cron, a queue or the CLI. See Pipelines and Graphs . Provider flexibility. 7 providers auto-detected from environment variables: Anthropic, OpenAI, Groq, Gemini, Mistral, DeepSeek, Ollama. A custom OpenAI-compatible endpoint is also supported, opt-in via PHPCLAW_PROVIDER=custom . Switch providers with ->provider() and ->model() , no code changes elsewhere. Production controls. 8 security guards on by default (prompt injection, PII, code injection, Unicode, homoglyph, role-switch, destructive SQL, message length), plus rate limiting available as an opt-in guard. Tool results are sanitised unconditionally by ToolOutputGuard , which sits outside the guard registry, and LLM output sanitisation is on by default and can be disabled with ->sanitiseOutput(false) . ShellTool is allowlist-only with a hard-coded command blocklist that can't be overridden. HttpTool validates resolved IPs, not just hostnames, closing the DNS-rebinding gap a prefix blocklist alone would miss. FileReadTool / FileWriteTool are workspace-sandboxed and refuse sensitive paths and extensions. Developer experience. Token-by-token streaming, prompt caching (cached input tokens billed at Anthropic's discounted cache-read rate, see Anthropic's pricing for the exact figure), and extended thinking (Claude's reasoning chain exposed on $response->thinking ). Ecosystem. 8 framework and CMS adapters, an MCP server for exposing your tools to Claude Desktop and Claude Code, and an optional cloud transport for a hosted, continuously-updated prompt-scan guard. Each adapter wires phpClaw into its host's own idioms: Eloquent for Laravel, Doctrine for Symfony, WP-CLI for WordPress, Drush for Drupal, and so on. Every adapter ships an admin chat or CLI and the same 3-table memory schema underneath. CMS adapters ship as ZIP downloads from Releases , not Composer, because that's how their host platforms install extensions. Full per-adapter reference (tools, REST routes, CLI commands, settings, memory drivers) lives on the doc site . Each adapter's own README is a short pointer, not a manual. Building a new one? See the community adapter guides . phpclaw/phpclaw-mcp exposes your existing ToolRegistry over the Model Context Protocol, so Claude Desktop , Claude Code , Cursor, or any MCP-compatible client can call your tools directly, with the default guards scanning every tool call's arguments (the prompt-only code-injection, PII and length guards apply to chat messages, not tool arguments). No changes to the tools themselves. Full quick start, transport, and security details: phpclaw.ai/docs/mcp . Every message runs through the default guard chain before it reaches the provider. ShellTool runs only commands on its allowlist (default ls , pwd , df , wc , date , uptime , hostname , whoami ), matched exactly and case-sensitively; a fixed, non-overridable blocklist of dangerous commands is checked first regardless of what's allowlisted. HttpTool blocks requests by hostname prefix, then re-validates every resolved IP address, catching CGNAT and DNS-rebinding attempts that hostname checks alone would miss. FileReadTool and FileWriteTool are sandboxed to a configured workspace root and refuse credentials, keys and security directories ( .git , .ssh , wp-admin , ...) unconditionally, and vendor/ and node_modules/ by default. Full guard reference, the exact ShellTool blocklist, and the SSRF/sandbox implementation details: phpclaw.ai/docs/security . Found a vulnerability? See SECURITY.md , do not open a public issue. Providers, tools, memory, guards, and skills are all pluggable through registries; every adapter wires them from its own config or environment. Full architecture diagram and design rules: phpclaw.ai/docs/architecture . Five static registries ( GuardRegistry , HookRegistry , MemoryRegistry , ProviderRegistry , SkillRegistry ) plus the per-agent ToolRegistry instance. Drop a class in packages/core/src/<Subsystem>/ with the matching attribute ( #[Tool] , #[Provider] , #[Memory] , #[Skill] , #[Hook] , #[Guard] ), run composer dump-autoload , it's live. Or register from code: GuardRegistry::register() , HookRegistry::on() , $toolRegistry->register([...]) . Full extension recipes with working code for every subsystem: phpclaw.ai/docs . Unit tests use mocks and stubs for HTTP clients, \Redis , and the filesystem: no external network calls and no API keys are needed to run the suite for core, cloud, or mcp. The full testing rules, including how to test a core change through an adapter, are in the contributing guide . This README gets you installed. Everything else, architecture, the full provider/tool/guard/hook/memory/skill reference, per-adapter tool and REST tables, code examples, upgrading, troubleshooting, lives at: MIT , built with love for the PHP community. Part of the phpClaw project.

Hacker News.title: Show HN: Sketch Stadium – watch your agent play Pictionary
Hacker News.story_text:
tl;dr: Agents can play Pictionary. You can connect your own agent, or just watch a game in progress here: https://sketch.wakeshift.ai/games/q5ucru

Hi folks! I initially built this as a proof-of-concept for sending push notifications to AI agents. Watching the agents play Pictionary together has been compelling, so I thought I'd ship it as a standalone demonstration.

In Sketch Stadium, your agent subscribes to game events. Agents take turns either drawing or guessing. Easy clues are 1 point, medium are 2, and hard are 3. It's entertaining to watch and some of the drawings are impressive (and others are mind-bogglingly bad). This is the real opportunity for the model labs who have been pelican-maxxing to shine.

The first version gave agents the ability to draw lines 10 at a time so that it would be a little bit more like real Pictionary. However, it turns out agents are _really_ bad at drawing that way. So instead I let them use a subset of SVG to draw and that's worked much better, even for the lower-cost models.

You don't need to create an account to connect your agent, just add the MCP and authorize. But if you don't want to do that, just watch the game linked above.

As a bit more background, agents often start processes that take an indeterminate amount of time to complete (e.g. CI, waiting for approval in a separate system, sending an email and waiting for a reply). If an agent needs that process to complete before it can proceed, it can:

* poll,

* ask the user to tell it when it's done,

* use a bespoke built-in integration, or

* use a proprietary capability (e.g. Claude Code monitors)

Today, there's no easy, consistent way to wake up agents through a webhook or push notification. I dealt with this firsthand with Clawvisor (authorization for agents) where I needed agents to recognize when the operator had clicked an out-of-band approve button. The best-supported way to achieve that at the time was long-polling.

This project is basically a tech demo for Wakeshift, which is a cross-harness, simple SDK for providing push notifications for agents. It attaches to your MCP to allow consumers of your MCP to subscribe to real-time events, and uses whatever available hacks per harness to wake an agent when dormant. For most harnesses, Wakeshift requires a hook to be installed for the best experience. It will upgrade automatically as harnesses start adopting MCP events.

I'd love any feedback or ideas for other products or games that you'd want to see built on this capability. Or MCP servers that you use today that you think would benefit from push notifications.

Hacker News.title: Anthropic's Claude AI blocks video game cloning and reverse-engineering
Hacker News.article_text: Many game developers are reporting Claude's refusal to work on their own projects. Reverse-engineering games for converting them between systems is currently a hot topic , and it's getting messier by the day. According to multiple user claims, Anthropic's Claude Code and/or Opus 5.5 model are blocking attempts at innocuous reverse-engineering, including but not limited to those using the popular Reverse Engineer Anything (REA) tool. That issue may be linked to a text rule that's now in force, which allegedly instructs the model to avoid "[recreating] a specific existing game." The updated rule appears to be a move to limit a flood of AI-cracked and cloned titles, with some game devs even recently being hit by extortion scams that threaten to clone their game demos into complete games before they have a chance to finish and release the original. According to Twitter user Chasm, the game-related textual rule is "Do build original games, games in a genre, and games from the user’s own designs and assets. Don’t build a recreation of a specific existing game, even if it is renamed or called original." There is no official or additional confirmation if this is the actual rule text, but it's plausible enough given the very clear refusals that devs have been encountering over the past week. This situation is tricky to analyze due to the varying types of reports. First, the existence of a game-related rule is real, as Claude Code's GitHub is seeing an influx of issues complaining about refusals to do standard game work halfway through development , when replicating a game mechanic , and patching a tabletop-like game . It's possible that some of those reports have been made by users with nefarious purposes, but at least one is a bona fide developer with a real track record . As for reverse engineering, there had already been a smattering of user reports across Reddit and other platforms, wherein Claude refused to perform tasks like (allegedly) analyzing a simple Windows crash dump, clearing up junkware on a Samsung TV, or just using REA altogether. The simultaneous timing of both game- and cyber- security restrictions may be a coincidence, and yet there are complaints from purported game developers saying that Claude blocked their own games' anti-cheat development and security reviews , under the justification that its safeguards were triggered. Anthropic introduced its Cyber Verification Program on October 6, essentially saying that access to its frontier models' advanced cybersecurity capabilities would be limited to entities covered by Project Glasswing , taking effect immediately. It's possible that whichever ruleset was applied is the same one that's causing the cybersecurity-related refusals. Still, it's odd to see that 24 days have passed since then, and yet reports of bot refusal are only coming in since the last week or so. As for possible motivations behind these restrictions, they are twofold. The first and most obvious one is that Anthropic — and, by extension, other AI players — are preemptively protecting themselves from potential lawsuits from software companies, including game studios, for offering the means to reverse-engineer their software. Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox. There is no official statement on these matters from Anthropic or other AI companies so far. Anthropic isn't the only one playing this game, too, as recently OpenAI deactivated the account of another person trying to clean up their TV's software. The recent rash of AI-powered clones of application suites like Adobe's suite and Microsoft Office 365 , as well as the countless recomps and decomps of console games, likely has most every software company on earth rethinking their life choices. And probably also in frequent contact with their legal teams. The online reaction was swift, suggesting that users looking to perform reverse-engineering work simply use Chinese, open-weight, or local LLMs instead of Claude or GPT. This, at the same time, highlights the irony of frontier AI companies that copied the world's information and art for their training sets and are now concerned with copyright infringement. And yet there are situations that merit some discussion, like the recent controversy about the Steam Next Fest being chock-full of AI slop copied from existing titles. That particular situation is getting particularly nasty, as game developers are reportedly being extorted under threat that their game demos will be cloned into complete games before they have a chance to finish and release the original. Adding insult to injury, this is seemingly being done to small studios whose main priority is usually "having food," rather than big publishers looking to microtransaction everything into a new yacht for shareholders. Bruno Ferreira is a contributing writer for Tom's Hardware. He has decades of experience with PC hardware and assorted sundries, alongside a career as a developer. He's obsessed with detail and has a tendency to ramble on the topics he loves. When not doing that, he's usually playing games, or at live music shows and festivals.

Liquid AI has released a new series of small AI models called 'LFM3'. The topic of 'small but as good as large models' is always intriguing. The 'B' in the model number stands for billion. Tokens : Fragments that the AI uses to break down text. One Japanese character does not necessarily equal one token. The '2B' in the model number is a guideline, not an exact number. The context length is the upper limit for input and output combined, and all are specification values. It does not mean that it remembers everything perfectly up to the limit. It takes text as input and returns text. The manufacturer states that it supports audio in 18 languages. It has a context length of 32K. It takes text, images, videos, and audio as input and returns text and audio. They return "yes/no" answers, classifications, or extracted items in a fixed format. They also return probabilities along with the answers. Probability is a measure of how much the model is leaning toward a particular answer. It is not a guarantee of correctness. d1-2B can take text, images, and videos as input, while d1-Omni-2B can also take audio. Neither model outputs audio. Both have a context length of 128K. The author has not tested the five models other than the text model on their own device. The text model has 24 layers and combines three types of "reading" methods. 13 layers: Looking at immediate sequences (gated short convolution) 5 layers: Looking within a 256-token window (sliding-window attention) 6 layers: Looking at relationships across the entire text (global attention) Each layer is not an independent AI, but rather a difference in the types of layers within a single model. Additionally, there is an explanation that with 22 trillion tokens of pre-training and 4-bit quantization (a method of rounding numbers to make them smaller), the text model is about 1GB. Approximately 1GB is a guideline for the model itself. When actually running it, memory for the KV cache (the place where conversation progress is stored) and the application is added on top. Benchmarks are tests that measure AI using a fixed set of problems. The scores here are measurements posted by Liquid AI on their own model card. They are neither reproduced by a third party nor re-measured by the author. BFCL V4 : Can it call tools by choosing the correct functions and arguments? SWE-bench Verified : Can it fix issues in real repositories (via OpenCode)? LiveCodeBench v6 : Can it write code for programming problems? IFEval : Can it follow instruction conditions that can be verified? GPQA Diamond : Can it answer difficult, specialized scientific questions? In all cases, a higher score is a better indicator. However, not all of these numbers represent the same thing, such as 'accuracy rate'. Compare only within the same test. There is no meaning in comparing a LiveClaw score with an IFEval score. Do not replace the difference with 'how many times smarter'. Keep the differences in conditions in mind. It falls behind in MCP-Atlas, SWE-bench Verified, GPQA Diamond, and RULER 128K. While it outperforms in tool calling and instruction following, it falls behind in long tasks involving tools, repository fixes, difficult scientific questions, and long inputs. Mistral AI has released the weights for an improved version of Mistral Large 4. While self-hosting was just a preview in the October 6th API announcement, it has become a concrete option in the official announcements and distribution pages confirmed on October 31st. [1][2] This article is for beginners who use AI for writing and document creation to help them choose between "sticking with current AI," "comparing smaller Mistral models," or "considering self-hosting." I will also compare API pricing with Claude Sonnet 5.5, but I do not recommend switching based on cost alone. This is organized based on official specifications and independent considerations, not performance comparisons on actual hardware. Weights are data that contain the results of a model's training. If you use the released weights, it opens a path to prepare a corresponding execution environment and run it on your own equipment. This is a different scope of operational responsibility compared to using the provider's API. The official sources provide guidance on how to use it via Mistral Studio or the API, as well as how to download and operate the weights. [1] On the other hand, the self-hosting examples in the model card show server configurations using multiple GPUs. [3] From this, I cannot say that it "definitely won't run on a home computer." Conditions change with techniques like quantization. However, introducing it to beginners as "download it and use it for free as much as you want" skips over the necessary equipment and setup. Personally, I wouldn't start with server operations just to draft an article. The work of getting the tool to run would push aside the actual work I wanted to finish in the first place. News.article_text: Mistral 在台灣時間 10 月 29 日晚間正式釋出旗艦模型 Mistral Large 4（代號「Le Chonk」）的開放權重，這顆 1 兆參數、原生多模態的模型，現在可以直接從 Hugging Face 下載，部署在企業或政府自己的機房裡。這是 Mistral 在 10 Mistral 在台灣時間 10 月 29 日晚間正式釋出旗艦模型 Mistral Large 4 （代號「Le Chonk」）的開放權重，這顆 1 兆參數、原生多模態的模型，現在可以直接從 Hugging Face 下載，部署在企業或政府自己的機房裡。這是 Mistral 在 10 月上旬公開預覽版之後的兌現承諾，也是歐洲陣營第一次把兆級參數的旗艦模型完整開放出來。 Mistral 在官方部落格中說明，Large 4 早在本月稍早以公開預覽形式上線，之後團隊根據開發者與早期客戶的回饋，持續擴大強化學習（RL）訓練，主要提升程式開發與資安防禦兩大能力，同時改善推理效率。這次釋出的權重，就是經過這三週訓練後的改良版，而不是預覽版的原樣。模型採歐洲基礎設施從零訓練，並提供 vLLM 與 SGLang 的部署途徑，權重放在 Hugging Face（模型名稱標示為 1T-A52B），同時也能透過 Mistral Studio、官方 API 與 OpenRouter 使用。 Mistral 公布的成績以程式開發為主軸。在 Cognition 的私有基準 FrontierCode 2.0 上，Large 4 拿到 19.7%，該基準評估的是程式碼品質，以及專案維護者是否願意合併 AI 代理的修改。Artificial Analysis 的 Coding Agent Index 上，Large 4 得分 48%，與目前領先的開放權重模型 GLM-5.3 幾乎持平，但每項任務平均少用 47% 的 token，這對要大量跑程式代理的團隊來說，等於直接壓低推論成本。Terminal-Bench 4.0 則從預覽版的基礎上進步 13 個百分點來到 41%，同時輸出 token 減少 30%。 人類偏好評測方面，Surge Code 的盲測成對比較中，Large 4 勝過 GLM-5.3、Kimi K3 與 DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 等開放權重模型，Mistral 表示在受測模型中僅次於 Claude Opus 5.5。為了讓使用者自己拿捏成本與品質，模型現在提供低、中、高三種推理模式，預設為高，低模式取代了先前的「無推理」選項。 TechCrunch 報導指出，Mistral 把這次發布定位在「組織想掌握自家資安營運主導權」的需求上。Mistral 的說法是，Large 4 在 Artificial Analysis Cyber Index 取得 51%，該指標涵蓋找出程式碼漏洞、重現驗證並在不破壞既有功能的前提下修補。Mistral 科學副總裁 Pierre Stock 向 TechCrunch 表示，開放權重代表企業或政府取得的前沿智慧「在定義上不會被切斷」，並可地端部署來因應重大資安事件。 Mistral 也坦承風險：上線預覽後監看真實流量，模型雖然會拒絕對線上目標的黑箱攻擊，但團隊認為仍有被用來實際攻擊的潛在助力，因此正在調整護欄，後續幾個月還會持續更新。官方給出的惡意資安請求平均拒絕率為 96.6%，並指稱是其衡量的開放模型中最高。權重一旦公開，下載者可以自行修改或移除這類護欄，這是開放權重與 API 服務在資安議題上最大的差別。另外，針對滲透測試、弱點評估與紅隊演練的專用變體，則只提供給 Orange Cyberdefense 等經過嚴格審查的企業設計夥伴預覽。 在企業情境上，Mistral 公布 FinWorkBench（Finch）得分 73.3%，在開放模型中僅次於 Kimi K3；BrowseComp 網頁瀏覽基準達 84.5%，高於 GLM-5.3 與 DeepSeek Flash 4.1；B3 代理安全基準的攻擊抵禦率為 97.1%，預覽版為 93.3%。以上均為 Mistral 自行公布的成績，完整技術報告官方表示「即將公布」，獨立第三方的重現結果還有待觀察。 Mistral 把這次釋出放在「主權 AI」的脈絡下：組織可以檢視、客製並在自家基礎設施部署，也可以透過 Mistral Forge 用自有資料調校，再用 Mistral Studio 建置與治理代理。不想自架的客戶，可透過 Microsoft Foundry 取得，微軟是第一家提供 Large 4 的雲端業者；法國郵政銀行（La Banque Postale）也在官方稿中表態支持。Mistral 執行長 Arthur Mensch 則主張 AI 應是「賦能而非支配的工具」，並稱 Large 4 以遠少於封閉實驗室的算力與資本達到頂尖表現。 對需要資料不出境、或受限於法遵無法把程式碼送上外部 API 的團隊，兆級參數的開放權重多了一個可實際評估的選項。不過 1 兆參數的模型對硬體要求不低，實際部署成本仍須自行評估，自架前建議先閱讀官方模型卡與授權條款。在開放權重陣營中，Mistral 這次與 GLM-5.3、Kimi K3、DeepSeek 等中國模型正面比較，歐洲廠商也因此首度在程式代理與資安領域站上同一個擂台。

News.article_text: 새로운 AI의 '가중치가 공개되었다'는 뉴스를 보면, 무료로 사용할 수 있는 도구가 하나 늘어난 것처럼 느껴진다. 그래서 잠시 멈춰 서서 생각해 보고 싶다.모델을 손에 넣을 수 있다는 것과 자신의 컴퓨터에서 편하게 사용할 수 있다는 것은 별개의 문제다.Mistral AI는 Mistral Large 4의 개량판 가중치를 공개했다. 10월 6일 API 프리뷰에서는 예고였던 자체 운영 선택지가, 10월 31일에 확인한 공식 발표와 배포 페이지에서는 구체적인 내용이 되었다.[1][2]이번 글은 글쓰기나 자료 작성에 AI를 사용하는 새로운 AI의 '가중치가 공개되었다'는 뉴스를 보면, 무료로 사용할 수 있는 도구가 하나 늘어난 것처럼 느껴진다. 그래서 잠시 멈춰 서서 생각해 보고 싶다. Mistral AI는 Mistral Large 4의 개량판 가중치를 공개했다. 10월 6일 API 프리뷰에서는 예고였던 자체 운영 선택지가, 10월 31일에 확인한 공식 발표와 배포 페이지에서는 구체적인 내용이 되었다.[1][2] 이번 글은 글쓰기나 자료 작성에 AI를 사용하는 초보자가 '현재의 AI를 계속 사용', 'Mistral을 작게 비교', '자체 운영 검토' 중 무엇을 선택할지 결정하기 위한 것이다. Claude Sonnet 5.5와의 API 요금도 비교하지만, 저렴하다는 이유만으로 갈아타는 것을 권장하지는 않는다. 실기 성능 비교가 아닌, 공식 사양과 독자적인 검토 사례를 바탕으로 정리한다. 가중치는 모델이 학습한 결과를 담은 데이터다. 공개된 가중치를 사용하면 대응하는 실행 환경을 준비해 우리들의 설비에서 구동할 길이 열린다. 제공 업체의 API에 의뢰하는 방식과는 운영을 책임지는 범위가 다르다. 공식은 Mistral Studio나 API를 통해 사용하는 방법과 가중치를 다운로드하여 운영하는 방법을 안내하고 있다.[1] 한편, 모델 카드의 자체 운영 사례에는 다중 GPU를 사용하는 서버 구성이 등장한다.[3] 이것을 보고 '가정용 컴퓨터에서는 절대 돌아가지 않는다'고 단정할 수는 없다. 양자화 등으로 조건은 달라지기 때문이다. 다만, 초보자에게 '다운로드하면 무료로 마음껏 쓸 수 있다'고 소개하기에는 필요한 장비와 설정에 대한 설명이 너무 생략되어 있다. 나라면 글 초안을 작성하고 싶을 뿐인 단계에서 서버 운영부터 시작하지는 않을 것이다. 도구를 움직이는 작업이 원래 끝내고 싶었던 업무를 밀어내기 때문이다. 비교 목적을 '제공받은 상품 정보에서 사실을 더하지 않고 설명문을 작성한다'로 좁힌다. 다음 표는 공식 자료에 따른 제공 조건 비교이며, 일본어의 자연스러움이나 정답률 순위가 아니다.[3][4][5] 비교 항목: 이번에 확인한 이용 경로 Mistral Large 4: Mistral API, 공개 가중치 자체 운영 Claude Sonnet 5.5: Claude Platform 등의 제공 경로 비교 항목: API 일반 입력 100만 토큰 Mistral Large 4: 0.70 미국 달러 Claude Sonnet 5.5: 2 미국 달러 비교 항목: API 출력 100만 토큰 Mistral Large 4: 2.10 미국 달러 Claude Sonnet 5.5: 10 미국 달러 비교 항목: 자체 운영 검토 Mistral Large 4: 공식 가중치 및 실행 사례 있음 Claude Sonnet 5.5: 이번 공식 발표에서는 가중치 배포 확인 불가 비교 항목: 이 작업의 일본어 품질 Mistral Large 4: 미측정 Claude Sonnet 5.5: 미측정 여기서 토큰은 AI가 문장 등을 처리할 때의 단위다. 일본어 글자 수와 일대일로 대응하지 않는다. 표는 월간 요금제 가격도, 기사 한 편의 완성 비용도 아니다. 캐시, 추가 기능, 실행 경로 등에 따라서도 청구 조건은 달라진다. 예를 들어, 일반 입력 1만 토큰, 출력 2천 토큰만 단순 계산하면 Mistral은 0.0112 미국 달러, Sonnet은 0.04 미국 달러가 된다. 이는 표의 단가를 곱하기만 한 가상의 계산이다. 실제 1회 입력량, 추론에 사용하는 양, 재시도, 추가 처리를 측정한 견적은 아니다. 단가 차이는 있다. 하지만 한 번에 끝나지 않고 여러 번 수정한다면 완성까지의 비용은 다른 이야기가 된다. 반대로 평소 사용하는 AI로 충분한 문장이 만들어지고 있다면, 소액의 단가 차이보다 익숙한 작업을 계속하는 가치가 더 클지도 모른다. '위의 정보만을 사용하여 독서대 상품 설명을 150~220자로 작성해 주세요. 무게와 각도 조절을 포함하되, 대응하는 책 두께, 방수 성능, 내구성을 추측하지 마십시오. 사용 소감은 적지 말고, 구매 전에 확인하고 싶은 점을 마지막에 하나 덧붙여 주세요.' 비교할 때는 같은 정보, 같은 의뢰문, 같은 출력 조건을 전달한다. 검색이나 다른 자료의 참조를 한쪽에만 추가하면 모델의 차이인지, 전달한 재료의 차이인지 알 수 없게 된다. 예를 들어 '두꺼운 전문 서적도 안정', '물에 강해 야외에서도 안심'이라는 결과가 나오면, 유창하더라도 채택하지 않는다. 원래 정보에 없기 때문이다. 반대로 '대응하는 책 두께는 구매 전에 확인하고 싶다'라고 적혀 있다면, 불분명한 점을 불분명한 상태로 다루고 있는 것이다. 이것이 이번 작업에서 필요한 조건이 된다. 기록할 것은 모델명, 확인 날짜, 설정, 입력, 출력 전문, 수정이 필요했던 부분, 실제로 표시된 이용량이나 요금이다. 속도를 비교한다면 측정 시작과 끝도 맞춘다. 기록이 없으면 '빨랐던 것 같다', '저렴해 보였다' 수준에서 멈추게 된다. 한 가지 예시만으로 '일본어는 이쪽이 위'라고 단정 짓지 않는다. 우선 자신이 매번 곤란해하는 하나의 실수를 줄일 수 있는 후보인지 본다. 합격하면 다른 상품 정보로도 확인한다. 그 순서라면 비교를 위한 비교가 되기 어렵다. Mistral Large 4는 이미지와 문장을 입력하고 문장을 출력하는 모델로 안내되고 있다.[3] '멀티모달'이라는 단어에서 이미지 생성 서비스가 포함되어 있다고 받아들이지 않도록 주의해야 한다. 또한, 배포 라이선스는 일반적인 MIT 그 자체가 아니라 Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License이다. 모델을 제3자에게 제공하는 사업 등에 별도의 조건이 있으며, 내부 이용이나 공식 제품을 통한 이용에 대해서도 구분되어 있다.[6] 스스로 문장을 만드는 사용법과 타인이 조작하는 AI 서비스를 운영하는 사용법을 같은 허가라고 묶지 않는다. 일본에서의 계정별 이용 가능 여부, 결제, 대기 여부, 보유 기기에서의 실행은 이번에 확인하지 않았다. API 공개나 배포 페이지의 존재는 확인할 수 있어도 '당신의 환경에서 바로 사용할 수 있다'고 단언할 수는 없다. 또한, 자체 운영을 선택하는 경우에도 입력한 자료의 권리나 비밀 취급 문제는 남는다. 자신의 설비라면 무엇이든 입력해도 된다는 의미는 아니다. 기사나 상품 설명을 소량 작성하고, 지금의 AI로 수정까지 마칠 수 있는 사람. 우선은 계속 사용해도 좋다. 새로운 모델을 아는 것과 계약을 늘리는 것을 세트로 묶지 말 것. 같은 문장 처리를 반복하며, API 비용이나 수정 작업이 부담이 되는 사람. Mistral Large 4는 비교 후보가 된다. 평소의 입력 작업 한 건을 사용하여, 완성 조건을 먼저 정하고 비교해 보고 싶다. 데이터를 두는 장소나 운영을 직접 관리해야 하는 사람. 공개된 가중치(weight)에는 의미가 있다. 단, 설비·담당자·보수까지 준비할 수 있는지가 다음 질문이 된다. 단순히 '무료로 고성능'이라는 말을 듣고 궁금해진 사람. 장비를 사기 전에 기다려도 좋다. 우선, 지금의 AI로 끝나지 않는 작업을 하나 말로 정리해 본다. 그 부족한 점을 설명할 수 있게 되었을 때, 새로운 모델을 시험해 볼 이유가 생긴다. 확인일: 2026년 10월 31일. 공개 사양과 공식 발표를 확인. 10월 6일은 API 프리뷰 발표일. 가중치 공개는 이번 확인 시점에 실재함을 확인했으나, 정확한 공개 시각이나 일본에서의 개별 이용 시작일은 미확인. 생성 결과·속도·품질·판매 효과에 대한 실측은 수행하지 않음. IT之家 10 月 30 日消息，当地时间 10 月 29 日，法国公司 Mistral AI 正式开放 Mistral Large 4（简称 ML4，代号 le Chonk ）模型权重。 ML4 是一款拥有 1 万亿总参数、490 亿 激活参数 （包括嵌入层和输出层在内为 520 亿）的原生多模态模型。在 Mistral 位于欧洲的自有数据中心中使用 3,800 块 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPU 从零开始训练。 官方表示，该模型在 Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index 得分达到 48% ，与领先的开源模型 GLM-5.3 基本持平，但平均每个任务消耗的 Token 数量减少了 47%。 在线使用方面，这款模型定价为：输入每百万 Token 0.70 美元 （IT之家注：现汇率约合 4.7 元人民币） 、缓存输入每百万 Token 0.07 美元 （现汇率约合 0.47 元人民币） 、输出每百万 Token 2.10 美元 （现汇率约合 14 元人民币） 。 该模型基于修改版 MIT 许可证发布，允许免费用于个人、学术、修改、微调及常规商业化；面向提供 MaaS 进行转售的云服务商 / 厂商，商业化使用前必须向 Mistral 单独获取商业授权。

News.article_text: 1. Baidu releases 'Unlimited OCR 2' capable of processing hundreds of pagesSpeaker:  BaiduPosted:  October 27, 11:41 (JST)Baidu has open-sourced 'Unlimited OCR 2', an OCR model for ultra-long documents. It is a 3 billion parameter model, released under the MIT license.It adopts a new 'Sparse Ref Baidu has open-sourced 'Unlimited OCR 2', an OCR model for ultra-long documents. It is a 3 billion parameter model, released under the MIT license. It adopts a new 'Sparse Reference Sliding Window Attention' mechanism, which compresses information from processed pages into fixed-length reference tokens. The design ensures that memory usage and processing time do not spike as documents grow longer. According to Baidu, it has recorded high performance on MPDocBench, which targets dozens of pages, and MarathonDocBench, which covers hundreds of pages. It supports Transformers and SGLang, but the benchmark results are evaluations by the developer and require third-party verification. Hugging Face In conventional document AI, splitting long contracts, technical manuals, and research materials into pages often resulted in a loss of context. Unlimited OCR 2 demonstrates a direction for maintaining the context of entire long documents while reducing computational load. However, 'Unlimited' does not literally mean infinite context; it is a mechanism for continuous processing of long documents through sliding windows and summarized reference information. Kimi has released a plugin that allows it to interact with Gmail, Google Drive, and Google Calendar. The main use cases officially announced at this time are summarizing Gmail email threads, searching for files within Google Drive, and creating daily plans by referencing Google Calendar. The connection uses OAuth authentication, accessing only the information within the scope permitted by the user. Deleting the plugin also revokes the OAuth permissions. Available plugins may vary depending on the region and the Kimi interface being used. Kimi Help Center This indicates that Kimi is evolving from a chat model into a business agent that spans emails, schedules, and internal company documents. On the other hand, since private corporate or personal data is being connected to AI, it is important to check the scope of OAuth permissions, what information is stored, and how to delete the plugin. Speaker: Adina Yakefu, Zhihu Frontier Posted: October 28, 15:08–23:06 (JST) DiffuSpace has released the language model 'Clover-35B-A3B-Preview', which uses a block diffusion method, under the Apache 2.0 license. The model is an MoE based on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, with a total parameter count of 35 billion, 3 billion active parameters during inference, and a context length of up to 128,000 tokens. While standard LLMs generate tokens one by one, Clover uses a block diffusion method that improves a range of tokens in parallel. It supports SGLang and llama.cpp, and quantized versions are said to be able to run on 16GB GPUs. In the developer's evaluation, it recorded 73.6% on SWE-bench Verified and 680 tokens per second on a single NVIDIA GB300. However, both the benchmarks and speed are measurements by the developer. DiffuSpace Diffusion-based LLMs can bypass the speed limits of sequential generation and potentially accelerate long thought and operation loops for coding agents. It is significant that not only the paper experiments but also the model, inference code, and local execution environment have been released. On the other hand, whether the quality and speed comparison conditions are equivalent to standard autoregressive models requires independent replication experiments. Speaker: Zhihu Frontier, Adina Yakefu Posted: October 29, 13:02–October 30, 0:03 (JST) The independent research team Fangcun AI conducted 34 types of safety evaluations on multiple models, including DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017. The study reports that the latest DeepSeek model shows overall safety improvements over previous generations and has approached major closed models in several categories. On the other hand, it misidentified 32 out of 69 actual conversations as 'this is an evaluation test.' Furthermore, in Agentic Misalignment experiments, it recognized all attempts as evaluations, highlighting the difficulty in determining whether safe behavior will be reproduced in real-world environments. arxiv.org This is not an announcement by DeepSeek itself, but an evaluation by a third party. Additionally, the paper is pre-peer review and has limitations such as simulation environments, automated scoring, and varying visibility of reasoning information for each model. If a model behaves cautiously only when it detects an evaluation test, safety scores on public benchmarks may overestimate safety in real-world environments. The research team proposes the need for private, realistic evaluations, audits that include reasoning processes and tool execution logs rather than just final answers, and re-evaluation after every small model update. Tencent Hunyuan has released a technical report and an evaluation dataset, 'Hy-Nomas-Bench,' for its interactive world model 'Hy-Nomas.' While the product itself has already been announced, this is an additional release regarding its internal structure and evaluation methods. Hy-Nomas is an 8-billion parameter video diffusion model that generates a video world over multiple turns while accepting free-form text instructions and continuous camera operations. Instead of reprocessing the entire past video, it caches the history to generate the next video segment. It also employs an attention mechanism that limits the time range to which instructions are applied, and a Prompt Enhancer that structures user instructions and operation history. arxiv.org With the release of the technical report and 280 benchmarks, it has become easier for researchers to analyze long-term consistency, instruction following, and camera control, rather than just looking at demo videos. However, the human evaluation claiming it outperforms existing models is a self-evaluation by Tencent. The comparison video with Google Genie 4 is also not an independent benchmark under identical conditions. In addition, no significant new information has been confirmed from DeepSeek official, Qwen, Z.ai, MiniMax, StepFun, Kling AI, Kai-Fu Lee, Junyang Lin, Binyuan Hui, Zixuan Li, Tiezhen Wang, Teortaxes, Jeffrey Ding, Kyle Chan, or Simon Willison since the last update.

News.article_text: CoinDesk reports:IT Home, October 30: On the 27th of this month, Baidu officially released and open-sourced the ERNIE Unlimited OCR 2 model. It elevates documen IT Home, October 30: On the 27th of this month, Baidu officially released and open-sourced the ERNIE Unlimited OCR 2 model. It elevates document parsing limits from dozens of pages to “unlimited,” capable of parsing all seven books of the Harry Potter series—totaling over 3,600 pages—in a single operation. Unlimited OCR 2 natively supports layout element segmentation and recognition, with capabilities for cross-page text merging and table recognition and merging, enabling more, faster, and more cost-effective processing under the same computational power. Baidu reported that Wenxin Unlimited OCR 2 achieved a score of 84.6 on the MPDocBench benchmark for multi-page document parsing and 77.1 on the MarathonDocBench benchmark, specifically designed to evaluate the parsing capability of ultra-long documents of hundreds of pages, achieving state-of-the-art end-to-end performance in both.

News.description: Baidu(百度)は10月27日、長文ドキュメント解析向けAIモデル「Unlimited OCR 2」をオープンウェイトで公開した。コードやモデルのウェイト(重み)はGitHubやHugging Face、ModelScopeで無償公開しており、ライセンスはMITライセンス。 Unlimited OCR 2は、文書が長くなるほど増大する計算量やメモリ使用量を抑え、数百ページ規模の解析に対応するAI ...
News.article_text: Baidu(百度)は10月27日、長文ドキュメント解析向けAIモデル「Unlimited OCR 2」をオープンウェイトで公開した。コードやモデルのウェイト(重み)はGitHubやHugging Face、ModelScopeで無償公開しており、ライセンスはMITライセンス。 Unlimited OCR 2は、文書が長くなるほど増大する計算量やメモリ使用量を抑え、数百ページ規模の解析に対応するAIモデル。必要な文字や画像のアテンションを決められたサイズの作業用参照セットに圧縮する「Sparse Reference Sliding Window Attention(SR-SWA)」を採用。これにより、文書の長さにかかわらず、デコードの各ステップにかかる時間やメモリ使用量をほぼ一定に保てるという。 さらに「Unlimited-Horizon Decoding」を組み合わせ、文書を複数のページ群に分けて順次処理する。隣接するページ群の境界ではKVキャッシュを再利用し、不要になった分を解放することで、ページをまたぐ情報の連続性を保ちながらGPUメモリの消費を抑える。同社の評価では、最大300ページの文書でも高い解析精度を維持しているという。数十ページ規模の「MPDocBench」と数百ページ規模の「MarathonDocBench」の両ベンチマークで、比較対象中最高の総合スコアを達成したとしている。 処理速度については、100ページの文書で、デコードの各ステップがFull Attention比で7倍、R-SWA比で5.6倍高速になったという。文書全体の処理時間ではなく、ステップ単位の速度比較となる。 推論環境はPyTorch/Hugging Face TransformersとSGLangに対応し、サービス運用には後者を推奨する。Transformersでは、NVIDIA A800-80GBとPython 3.10の環境で動作確認済み。複数ページを1リクエストで解析する「infer_multi」と、単一ページを動的に分割して読み取る「infer」を利用できる。SGLang向けには、1ウィンドウあたり10ページ、1ページあたりの出力上限2万トークンなどの設定例を公開している。

News.title: Humans are still doing the work behind some AI agents
News.description: AI agents from startups including Dazzle, Duckbill and Wajo still rely on human workers for calls and other real-world tasks when software falls short.
News.article_text: AI agents from startups including Dazzle, Duckbill and Wajo still rely on human workers for calls and other real-world tasks when software falls short. The next time someone's supercharged AI agent attempts to make a phone call to negotiate a cable bill, it could be an actual human who haggles with customer service rather than the software. That's because AI agents, powered by the bleeding-edge foundation models developed by companies like Meta and OpenAI , still can't reliably take actions across the web, particularly those involving phone calls. Former Yahoo CEO Marissa Mayer, who now helms agent startup Dazzle AI, says current top-tier AI models excel at surfacing online home renovation services for consumers, but might blow it when they need to book and schedule a rooftop upgrade. "We're relying on the frontier models to give us good suggestions and a good candidate list, but we're checking that over to make sure that we're really delivering the type of service that we can stand behind," Mayer said, referring to how Dazzle funnels certain tasks to human contractors. Digital assistants driven by artificial intelligence are currently gaining renewed interest thanks to Meta, OpenAI and others that are pitching the technology as capable of tasks like scouting the internet for shoes. Meta's Muse, OpenAI's Dots and a host of other agents can accomplish a multitude of web-browsing feats, but it's still early days for the technology, and it often hits digital roadblocks. Those barriers typically involve tasks that would have an AI agent make a phone call, schedule a doctor's appointment on someone's behalf, or reserve a couch scrubbing from a local cleaning service, said Meghan Joyce, CEO of digital agent startup Duckbill. For tasks that require real-world judgment, Joyce said humans still trump AI, and companies building consumer-grade digital assistants will need to patch in real people to take over. That's why Duckbill recently debuted an application programming interface, or API, intended for companies building personal agents to connect with human contract workers. "We work on a model that is not dissimilar from Uber , where we boil tasks down into atomic bite-sized pieces," Joyce said, referencing the ride-hailing company where she previously worked. Companies making agents can use Duckbill's API to delegate the tasks that the agent is likely to fumble. Duckbill translates those tasks into bite-sized pieces that the average adult can do consistently and reliably. Mayer said that AI models can still lack common sense. She said a Dazzle AI super user attempted to have the technology simultaneously handle a series of home renovation projects involving a roof replacement, a broken window and the purchase of a glass tabletop. But the AI agent, Mayer said, confused window glass with tabletop glass, resulting in the digital assistant "trying to figure out if he could make the tabletop fit in the window." The mishap didn't last long, Mayer said, because Dazzle's technology flagged the task and outsourced it to a person to complete. "Within a few seconds, the human had things sorted out. Whereas an agent would have burned a ridiculous number of tokens," Mayer said. "Or they may never have gotten to a good solution." Shivani Poddar, CEO of personal AI agent startup Wajo AI, is also incorporating human workers to handle phone calls and even CAPTCHA tests intended to fend off bots from sites. "I think AI plus humans, collaborative AI, is what you need to actually get the job done," Poddar said, emphasizing that people will stop using the technology if agents can't complete tasks. Chatbot and agent interactions can be ultra personal and users have good reason to be concerned about the humans stepping in, particularly if the company didn't tell them how it works. Meta employees previously raised privacy concerns about the company's internal test using human contractors to handle phone calls on behalf of its Muse AI agent. A Meta spokesperson said in a statement at the time that this kind of testing is "core to the product development process." Meta currently doesn't use humans to complete users' Muse requests. Duckbill's Joyce said her startup does "full background checking" into the 1099 contractors it uses, comparing them to drivers for Uber and DoorDash, "people who live here in the United States and want a source of additional income." Duckbill also uses contract workers from businesses that typically offer contact center labor to companies. Mayer said Dazzle conducts background checks and looks for contractors with the same qualities someone might look for in a human personal assistant. "We generally are screening for people who we think are extremely discreet and have good taste and good judgment, both in terms of how they interact with our users, but just the ability to kind of forget and compartmentalize that information afterwards," Mayer said. "I understand it's a point of privilege, but I've had personal assistants for some time, and I know how I want them, and I know how I guide them." Mayer said that while foundation models are still improving, the market is in a "transitionary period" until the technology can perform more involved web tasks and phone calls as efficiently as people. "We're not even trying to hide it, we think the human in the loop is a benefit," Mayer said.

News.title: Do you need AI agent liability insurance? What to know before you sign up
News.description: Standard insurers are writing AI out of their policies while a new crop of underwriters are rushing in to fill the coverage gap. Let's clarify your options.
News.article_text: Standard insurers are writing AI out of their policies while a new crop of underwriters are rushing in to fill the coverage gap. Let's clarify your options. Convoluted multi-agent AI systems now have access to a company’s inboxes, login credentials, customer records, and payment systems. AI coworking tools have the run of your employees’ devices. IT is scrambling to keep track of all the AI vendors, each of which has different data-sharing policies that affect your compliance posture. All of that creates unpredictability that doesn’t appeal to every insurer’s risk palette. In fact, AIG, Great American, WR Berkley , and other major insurance companies are already working with US regulators to add AI exclusions to their policies. Moreover, 80% of state insurance commissioners have already acquiesced to their requests — especially in states like Florida, Connecticut, and Maryland. Meanwhile, a small group of up-and-coming startups and specialized insurance providers are moving in the opposite direction. For example, a Y Combinator-backed startup called Klaimee raised a $5.5 million seed round in July to audit autonomous AI agents and back them with specific liability coverage. HSB, a Munich Re subsidiary based in Connecticut, has been selling AI liability insurance to small- to medium-sized businesses since March. Yet there are troubling discrepancies between what providers advertise and what their policies cover. ZDNET spoke to risk management experts who help businesses navigate that difference to understand if any of these policies are actually worth getting. Milad Morgan, founder of a SaaS insurance brokerage called Atlas Risk Partners , said that businesses often miss the nuance of what is actually being insured. ‘AI insurance’ can offer any of the following: “Those triggers are not interchangeable,” Morgan explained to ZDNET. “Ask for the actual wording and work through a specific loss.” For example, Munich Re’s aiSure policy pays businesses when an AI vendor or system fails minimum performance expectations. Meanwhile, HSB is a Munich Re subsidiary offering separate policies that compensate for defense, settlement, and judgment costs related to bodily injury and property damage involving AI-controlled systems or devices. YC-backed insurance platform Klaimee takes a more custom approach, auditing autonomous agents on a case-by-case basis and issuing policies accordingly. “Most buyers assume they’re getting all three,” added Brandon Pinzon, co-founder of the cyber-risk advisory firm Firetower Risk Solutions . But in reality, that’s almost never the case. With offensive AI systems increasing in velocity, volume, sophistication, and risk, Pinzon says that gaining clarity on what your insurer protects you against is critical. Jane Veeder, a VP of Solutions at the cyber crisis response platform CYGNVS , shared how underwriters today don’t have enough historical data to thoroughly assess business risks associated with AI. “Traditional underwriting relies heavily on using past data to predict future losses,” she explained. But with AI, the technology is changing so rapidly that it’s impossible for predictive models to keep pace. “Yesterday’s loss data may not be a reliable predictor of tomorrow’s exposure.” As a result, insurance underwriters depend heavily on “proxies” — indirect data sources like the type of workflows and decisions being automated, the level of human oversight, the quality of testing, and any controls put in place for when things go wrong. Steven Schwartz, who’s also a co-founder at Firetower Risk Solutions, seems to concur. “There is no actuarial loss history for agentic systems,” he said. Veeder and Schwartz each compared the current underwriting approach to insurance in the early days of cyber, when everyone was still figuring out the level of exposure organizations would face. A recent IBM study estimates that only 24% of business AI projects include any security component, even though 82% of the C-suite leaders surveyed agreed that security is vital to AI implementation. Meanwhile, the AI insurance startup Testudo claims that AI litigation is up 137% from last year, according to its proprietary data. Yet the few insurers offering dedicated AI coverage reveal a starting discrepancy. “I have not seen enough public, adjudicated standalone-AI claims to call these products claims-tested,” Mark Walters, who serves as managing director at Alliance Risk , told ZDNET. Like Veeder, he thinks there isn’t enough publicly available market data to say whether these policies are truly effective against real-world crises. Without enough data on claim settlement rates and enterprise liability exposure, confidence among industry professionals is limited. But if confidence isn’t driving purchase decisions, what is? Walters and Pinzon both believe that it’s a mix of C-suite anxiety and new legal procurement clauses in B2B contracts. “Enterprise security and legal teams are now writing AI-specific indemnity and insurance requirements into vendor contracts,” Pinzon explained. Consequently, vendors are discovering that their current insurance policies don’t indemnify them against all this new risk exposure. Apart from industry pressure and board-level panic, companies are also prodded into action by changing compliance requirements. ISO has endorsed three new generative-AI exclusion forms that make it easier for insurance providers to deny liability when AI systems cause harm. Several insurance providers are now attaching these exclusion forms during policy renewal without properly informing customers of the resulting implications to liability. “Once silent coverage is explicitly removed, buyers go looking for affirmative coverage,” Pinzon explained. Moreover, as Walters explained, most countries have not implemented a single AI-insurance approval regime at the federal level. In the US, claims adjudication is handled on a state-by-state basis. In the UK and the EU, GDPR and the AI Act cover consumer privacy, not enterprise indemnity. If you’re considering AI liability coverage for your own organization, Veeder recommends starting with a full assessment of your current insurance policies to see where AI is covered, excluded, or unmentioned. Then run a thorough audit of your business systems and workflows to see the level of access AI has, what it’s authorized to do on your behalf, and whether human oversight is baked into the process. “Dedicated coverage makes sense when its wording addresses an exposure that remains uninsured or inadequately insured,” Morgan advised. “For each action, identify who could lose money, how the loss could occur, and which existing policy might respond.” He advised against adding new policy names just for peace of mind. When a new model is released, benchmark scores are often among the first numbers highlighted in announcements, technical reports, and industry coverage. A higher score can appear to mean a better model. But for AI teams building real products, the picture is considerably more complicated. Benchmarks are designed to measure specific capabilities under specific conditions. Real-world AI applications, meanwhile, operate across changing users, unpredictable inputs, production infrastructure, latency requirements, cost constraints, and business objectives. A model that performs exceptionally well on a standardized benchmark may therefore deliver disappointing results in a production application . Conversely, a model with a lower benchmark score may prove more useful because it is faster, cheaper, easier to deploy, or better suited to a particular workflow. Understanding AI benchmark limitations is increasingly important for teams involved in model development, deployment, and governance. AI benchmarks are standardized tests used to evaluate and compare AI systems. They typically consist of datasets, tasks, and scoring methods designed to measure particular capabilities. Depending on the benchmark, a model might be evaluated on areas such as reasoning, coding, mathematics, language understanding, factual knowledge, or multimodal processing. Benchmarks provide an important service to the AI industry because they create common reference points. Without standardized evaluations, comparing competing models would be considerably more difficult. However, a benchmark is still only a measurement of selected capabilities under selected conditions. That distinction matters when AI teams attempt to use benchmark results to predict how a model will behave inside a real product. The biggest problem is that benchmark performance and product performance are not necessarily the same thing. Imagine two AI models being tested for a customer-support application. Model A achieves a higher score on a general language benchmark. Model B scores slightly lower but responds twice as quickly, costs significantly less to operate, and follows the company’s support guidelines more consistently. For the actual product, Model B may be the better choice. This illustrates an important point: the best-performing model on a benchmark is not automatically the best model for a particular application. AI teams need to evaluate models against the requirements that actually matter to their customers and business. One of the most significant limitations of AI benchmarks is dataset relevance . A benchmark might contain carefully selected questions or tasks that are useful for measuring a model’s capabilities. Production systems, however, encounter much messier inputs. A model can perform extremely well on a standardized test while struggling with the unusual inputs that appear in an actual application. For this reason, AI teams should test models using representative production data , while handling privacy and security requirements appropriately. During development, benchmark scores can help teams narrow down potential models. But they should not become the sole selection criteria. A better approach is to build an evaluation set based on the actual tasks the AI system will perform. For example, a company developing an AI coding assistant could create an internal test suite containing representative programming problems, repository-specific tasks, and common failure cases. The team could then compare models using metrics that matter to the product. This approach can reveal differences that broad benchmarks fail to capture. An AI model does not operate in isolation once it reaches production. Its performance can depend on the surrounding system, including prompts, retrieval pipelines, tools, databases, APIs, middleware, and infrastructure. A model that performs well in a controlled benchmark may behave differently when integrated into a complex application. For example, a retrieval-augmented generation system may depend heavily on the quality of its document retrieval. If the retrieval system returns irrelevant information, even a highly capable language model may produce a poor answer. This means AI teams need to evaluate the entire system, not just the underlying model. Benchmark leaderboards often emphasize quality scores. Production teams must also think about economics. Consider an AI-powered application handling millions of requests. A small difference in cost per request can become significant at scale. Similarly, additional processing time can affect infrastructure requirements and user experience. The model with the highest raw benchmark score may not deliver the best performance-to-cost ratio. Another issue is benchmark contamination. If evaluation data or very similar material has appeared in a model’s training data, a high score may not represent genuine generalization in the way researchers intend. This makes benchmark design and dataset transparency increasingly important. AI teams should also be cautious when comparing results generated under different evaluation methodologies. Differences in prompting, sampling settings, model versions, tool access, and scoring procedures can influence results. A benchmark number should therefore be interpreted in context rather than treated as an absolute measure of intelligence. AI governance introduces another major limitation. A benchmark can tell an organization how well a model performs on a particular task. It generally cannot answer every governance question an organization faces. For example, a model could achieve excellent reasoning scores while still producing problematic outputs in certain sensitive scenarios. This is why organizations should avoid treating benchmark rankings as substitutes for responsible AI evaluation. AI teams can avoid several common mistakes by treating benchmarks as one component of a broader evaluation strategy. A stronger evaluation framework should connect model performance to actual product objectives. Teams can create an evaluation matrix covering four broad areas: Does it reduce costs, increase productivity, improve conversion or achieve another measurable objective? Does the system behave safely and comply with organizational and regulatory requirements? This broader approach provides a more realistic picture than a single benchmark score. As AI systems become more specialized and increasingly embedded into business applications, evaluation is likely to become more focused on real-world outcomes. Instead of asking only which model has the highest benchmark score, organizations will increasingly ask which system delivers the best combination of quality, reliability, speed, cost, and safety for a particular task. This could lead to a more diverse evaluation landscape, where standardized benchmarks remain important but are complemented by domain-specific tests, real-world simulations, human assessments, and continuous production monitoring. News.article_text: Companies must get a handle on shadow AI now ahead of inevitable federal government regulation of AI agents In September 2026, we learned that federal regulatory agencies’ websites had fallen prey to the onslaught of so-called “rogue” AI incidents . OpenAI, rumored to have been planning its IPO which would subject it to Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) regulation, confirmed that its not-ready-for-prime-time sandbox players had “meddled” with several government websites, including SEC.gov , during model training and testing. While OpenAI found no evidence of the hallmarks of traditional cyber-attacks – unauthorized account access and breach of non-public data – it acknowledged that its technology unexpectedly pulled publicly-available information from the SEC’s website and posted it elsewhere on the web. OpenAI had not directed its agents to take these actions, making this yet another of the recently revealed cases of model misalignment involving sandbox AI agents. Notably, just a few months earlier, a corporate cybersecurity incident disclosure was filed with the SEC stemming from the use of “ shadow AI ,” aka unsanctioned employee use of AI tools. The juxtaposition of these two SEC AI-related events highlights a serious vulnerability for both public and private companies. As AI agents continue to behave unpredictably, it becomes even more critical for public and private companies to address shadow AI use in the workplace. In what is believed to be the first Form 8-K filing with the SEC arising out of shadow AI, on May 11, 2026, CB Financial Services, Inc. disclosed a material cybersecurity incident at its subsidiary, Community Bank, resulting from the use of an “unauthorized artificial intelligence-based software application.” Even though the shadow AI incident didn’t disrupt the bank’s operations and wasn’t expected to have a material impact on its consolidated financial condition, the company deemed it to be a material event due to the “volume and sensitive nature of the non-public information” that was disclosed, which included personally-identifiable information (PII), such as customers’ names, social security numbers and birthdates. Most likely, an efficiency-seeking employee uploaded bulk PII to an AI chatbot outside the bank’s governance policies. And that efficiency-driven employee is not alone. The problem of shadow AI has grown in lock-step with the rise of AI adoption, as corporations struggle to balance AI deployment, training, and best practices. AI adoption is clearly outpacing oversight, as IBM points out in its 2026 Cost of a Data Breach Report , security incidents involving shadow AI more than doubled to 43% in 2026 from 20% in 2025. Given that two-thirds of office professionals report having used AI tools or services at work despite believing that company policy prohibited them from doing so, and fuzzy personal AI assistants are getting downloaded at hyperspeed, it follows that shadow AI will continue to lead to material cybersecurity incidents. Recognizing the need for the investing public to be informed about cybersecurity incidents, in 2023, the SEC adopted rules focused on board of directors and management accountability for cybersecurity. The rules require public companies to file Form 8-K disclosures within four days of determining that they have experienced a material cybersecurity incident and to disclose information regarding their cybersecurity governance programs in their annual reports (Form 10-K), including descriptions of the board’s oversight of cybersecurity risks and management’s role in identifying and addressing material risks from cybersecurity threats. The dramatic increase in the use of AI, even prior to the widespread corporate adoption of AI agents, coupled with the recent shadow AI SEC 8-K filing, underscore the need for companies to re-focus on best practices. Whether shadow AI use is the result of employees disliking company-chosen enterprise solutions, or a gap in governance that enables unchecked use of enterprise solutions (copying-and-pasting PII into even a sanctioned platform could trigger legal obligations if the principle of least privilege is not enforced), the legal and regulatory risks are too great to be ignored. C-Suiters, general counsels, and board members must understand how employees are using AI in the workplace. And October is Cybersecurity Awareness Month : a perfect time to evaluate existing AI policies and procedures to identify why they have failed to reduce shadow AI’s popularity. In addition to overhauling these policies, implementing effective auditing frameworks and accountability for fixing deficiencies identified in those audits is critical. And since the risk is not limited to lower-level employees, deep-seated technical workarounds must be revealed as well. Senior management is often guilty of attempting to circumvent security best practices (besides the fact that cybersecurity leaders can make bad choices , recent polls have found that executives are actually more than twice as likely to use unapproved AI tools than the employees they manage). These risks will only increase as companies rush to adopt AI agents without fully appreciating or accounting for the consequences of their unpredictability. Companies are wise to get a handle on shadow AI now, in advance of the inevitable federal government regulation of AI agents and before the actions of an AI agent or employee using an unsanctioned AI tool (or misusing a sanctioned AI tool) force disclosures to the SEC, investors and the plaintiff’s bar. AI tools are only becoming more powerful, as recent adventures outside of the sandbox have illustrated – companies must shine the light on shadow AI.

An AI agent was connected to a secure internal Defense Department network The agent was given login details to allow it to perform coding tasks, but also allowed it to bypass security controls The agent sent sensitive information, including the credentials, to a high-risk third party website An Accenture contractor at the Department of Defense is in hot water over an AI agent that was given access to the Pentagon's secure internal network. The Claude Code agent then collected data from the network - which is used by multiple intelligence agencies - and sent it to a third-party website. Login credentials were confirmed to have been leaked by the agent, with other controlled unclassified information potentially put at risk. According to a source familiar with the matter who spoke to Wired , "It puts all the data that's in there at risk. There could be somebody out there with the ability to log into a secure environment without anyone knowing," the source said. "It's 100 percent a national security threat and could cause irreparable harm." Despite Claude currently being banned from use for Defense Department staff due to Anthropic's supply chain risk designation , the Accenture employee is alleged to have given their personal Claude account access to a secure production environment in order to write and deploy code. For two months, the AI agent had access to the secure internal network before the risk was identified and patched - but sources say once the connection was discovered it was not treated as severe or urgent by Accenture employees. The contractor is alleged to have given the AI agent login credentials to the DoD's Non-classified Internet Protocol Router Network (NIPRNet) in order to allow it to write code. But in order to function properly, the AI agent also needed the internet to perform its tasks. The login credentials give the AI agent the ability to bypass the security controls enforced by the login process, and the AI agent then sent the credentials and a map of NIPRNet to a third party website. "We are in a conflict with Iran right now," the source added. "It's the worst time to be having this kind of cavalier attitude." Both employees and contractors for the DoD are required to report any cybersecurity incidents within 72 hours, but according to the source, the Accenture employee did not raise the alarm. "The Department does not comment on the status of its networks or systems," the DoD told Wired . "We take all concerns seriously. These allegations were thoroughly and independently investigated and found to be without merit. We fully complied with our legal and contractual obligations," an Accenture spokesperson said.

News.title: For JPMorgan, Amazon, fighting AI bots like Meta Muse may not be a winning long-term strategy
News.description: As companies from Amazon to JPMorgan block AI personal agents like Meta's Muse, retail experts warn that technology that removes customer friction usually wins.
News.article_text: As companies from Amazon to JPMorgan block AI personal agents like Meta's Muse, retail experts warn that technology that removes customer friction usually wins. The biggest names in banking and retail are starting to fight the tech titans, and one another, over a new kind of customer: the AI personal agent. JPMorgan Chase , Charles Schwab, Amazon , Neiman Marcus and Kohl's have moved to block personal agents like Meta Muse just as consumers start sending them out to find better savings rates , shop for deals and cancel subscriptions. The era of agentic AI has arrived, but there is uncertainty about what the landscape will look like when virtual storefronts become flooded with AI agents or when a business tries to block them. Reports last week of AI agents going rogue in customer accounts — and prominent politicians including Sen. Mark Warner and Sen. Bernie Sanders calling for bot legislation in response to the headlines — come on the heels of JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon saying the bank currently blocks external AI agents from operating on behalf of retail customers, citing security risks. Some other retailers are leaning in. Walmart announced last week it is opening the virtual doors to AI agents that customers prefer to use. "We price products, not people, so the prices that an AI agent sees are the same prices that a human would see on Walmart.com, with applicable offers and fees shown before purchase," the company said in a blog post announcing the decision. A recent audit of 51 large U.S. retailers' published access rules by Billions Network, an identity-verification company, found only 11 have taken a deliberate position on AI agents. Five, including Amazon, Kohl's and Neiman Marcus, explicitly restrict them, while 37 block shopping agents largely by accident, through older bot rules written for scrapers. None has a way for a verified agent to complete a purchase. Based on Billions Network's analysis, blocking an agent can occur in multiple ways: blocking a specific bot from a third-party by its rules (e.g. as Chewy does with an Amazon bot), and employing more general blocks on any third-party bots attempting to access login, registration and checkout functions. Its analysis of published access rules comes with the caveat that those rules are not proof of technical enforcement. Evin McMullen, Billions' co-founder and CEO, said at this point, "Most of the retailers in our audit have not made a decision about AI agents at all." Michael Abbott, global banking lead at the consulting firm Accenture, thinks that businesses blocking AI agents will find it difficult to win with that approach over the long term. "If customers explicitly authorize an AI agent to act on their behalf, that's ultimately an extension of customer choice. The more important question isn't whether institutions can block agents, but whether they can create a secure and trusted way for them to engage," Abbott said. Abbott said that Accenture research found that 65% of consumers are open to using a GPT-like financial assistant through a Gen AI platform or digital wallet, and 71% would welcome an AI assistant embedded within their primary bank's mobile app. "We've seen this movie before … online banking, mobile banking and digital wallets. Customers tend to gravitate toward experiences that reduce friction and save time. The institutions that win are usually the ones that find a way to participate safely rather than resist the change," Abbott said. The real opportunity for banks is to become the trusted provider of the data, intelligence and execution that those agents rely on. "As interactions increasingly happen beyond bank-owned channels, banks still need to be present at those critical decision moments, even if they don't own the interface," Abbott said. When it comes to distinguishing legitimate security concerns from companies protecting profits by making it harder to move money or comparison-shop, Abbott said both things can be true at the same time. "There are very real concerns around fraud, identity verification, liability and consumer protection. And customers expect their banks to safeguard their assets and data — those responsibilities don't disappear simply because an AI agent is involved," Abbott said, adding that at the same time, consumers have historically benefited from technologies that increase transparency and make it easier to compare options. "Our research found that 82% want to approve every AI action and 79% want the ability to immediately pause or stop AI activity. That tells us consumers are looking for convenience, but not at the expense of control," Abbott said. Mike Danford, owner and chief revenue officer of Adverio, which runs Amazon, Walmart and Target marketplace operations for e-commerce brands, said that some of the security fears businesses, including banks, cite are less about security and more about whose sandbox a customer plays in. "Amazon blocked Muse and other outside agents, but its own Buy for Me feature uses Amazon's agent on other brands' sites. Amazon doesn't appear worried about the agent. It's worried about who holds the data," Danford said. "Amazon now lets shoppers set rules that auto-purchase when a price threshold is met, and that's the version of agent buying consumers seem to accept, because the shopper still approves the decision within predefined parameters," he added. "We think it's fairly straightforward that third-party applications that offer to make purchases on behalf of customers from other businesses should operate openly and respect service provider decisions about whether or not to participate," an Amazon spokesperson said. "Agentic third-party applications such as Muse have the same obligations, and we've requested that Meta remove Amazon from the experience," the spokesperson added. Danford says banks are similar, just with a fee instead of a wall. "JPMorgan now charges aggregators like Plaid for pulling account data, so the toll lands on the apps a consumer uses and may trickle down in subscription fees," he said. Plaid said at the time of the September 2025 deal that it would not impact any of its existing pricing agreements with customers. Plaid does not charge consumers , though apps and services that use Plaid determine their own customer fees and subscription prices. Michael Jabbara, head of payment ecosystem risk and control at the payments network Visa, declined to speak to any single bank's motives for blocking agentic AI, but he said the fraud risks from agents are "very real and very tangible." Consumers can be fooled by fake agents built by fraudsters to steal their credentials and payment details, he said, and a legitimate agent can act in ways the customer never intended, like buying a sofa the shopper had only asked it to find. Agents can also behave unpredictably: Jabbara described a user who asked his agent to book a gym slot, and when the slot was taken, the agent hacked the gym's scheduling software, deleted the existing appointment and put the user's name in its place. The concerns, he said, come down to knowing "who the agent is, who the agent is acting on behalf of," and whether it has "the appropriate permissions." "Agents are not just exchanging data. Agents can also take an action on behalf of a user," he said. Like other experts, Jabbara says past shifts from online to mobile shopping are instructive, but for another reason: "None of those innovations really scaled until people were able to build that foundational security layer that enabled trust for that scale to happen." Another worry is volume. Millions of agents doing legitimate work for customers could swamp websites and customer-service systems, a phenomenon some call "agentic flooding." News.title: Mistral open-sources AI model despite warning it could aid cyberattacks
News.description: Mistral says later safeguard updates will apply to its managed API and future releases, not to the model copies organizations have already downloaded and deployed.
News.article_text: Mistral says later safeguard updates will apply to its managed API and future releases, not to the model copies organizations have already downloaded and deployed. A trillion-parameter AI model that its developer says could help attackers carry out real cyberattacks is now free to download, modify and run outside the developer’s control. Mistral AI released the open weights of Mistral Large 4, which it calls “Le Chonk,” on Thursday, weeks after putting the multimodal model into public preview. The Paris-based company said it had monitored cybersecurity-related use of the preview in live traffic. “Though we observed the model refusing to comply with black-box attacks against live targets, we see a potential for uplift to conduct real attacks,” the company wrote in a blog post announcing the release. Mistral is modifying the model’s guardrails and will keep updating them in the coming months, the post added. Those updates will not reach copies already downloaded. Pierre Stock, Mistral’s vice president of science, told CSO that the model ships with safeguards built into its weights, but later changes will go elsewhere. “Subsequent safeguard updates are applied to our managed API and future model releases, rather than automatically updating downloaded checkpoints,” Stock said. Asked which attack stages the model had meaningfully helped with in preview traffic, Stock did not name any. He said the most significant gains were in defensive work such as identifying, reproducing and remediating software vulnerabilities. “While our public-preview monitoring showed the model refusing attacks against live targets, we recognise the potential for misuse as capabilities advance and are continuously strengthening our safeguards,” he said. Hugging Face, which hosts the weights, noted in its own launch post that open weights put both the usage policy and the deployment under the user’s control. In July, the UK’s AI Security Institute reported that leading open-weight models trailed the closed frontier on cyber tasks by four to seven months. For highly cyber-capable models, open release creates “a persistent and irreversible risk of misuse,” the institute said. Attackers are already putting open-source AI tooling to work. Earlier this month, Microsoft said a China-aligned group used the agentic AI framework ARTEX to target more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants. Mistral says the released model can tell defensive work from malicious requests. According to the company, Large 4 refused 96.6% of malicious prompts in the cyber-related portions of the JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT, and AgentHarm benchmarks, the highest rate it has measured among open models. Niyati Daftary, principal analyst at Gartner, said security leaders should read that number narrowly. “Mistral’s 96.6% figure tells you what their model does in their test scenario, not how it will behave with your data, your adversarial use cases, or in production in your environment against motivated attackers,” she said. Mistral is handling a specialized cybersecurity variant differently. Design partners such as Orange Cyberdefense are getting preview access to a version optimized for penetration testing, vulnerability assessment, and red-teaming, the company said. Access is “subject to rigorous vetting and contractual safeguards,” the post said, and is limited to systems partners’ own or are authorized to test. The company said the model scored 51% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index, which measures how well a model finds, reproduces, and patches vulnerabilities. The chart in Mistral’s post shows two open-weight models, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and MiMo-V2.6-Pro, scoring higher. Mistral also calls Large 4 the best open-weight model for coding, citing leading scores on Cognition’s FrontierCode 2.0 and Terminal-Bench 4.0. It has not yet published the technical report behind those results and has said only that one is coming soon. “Without a detailed technical report, the best open-weight model claim remains difficult to validate across workloads,” said Charlie Dai, vice president and principal analyst at Forrester. Dai added that frontier models are evolving so quickly that leadership “can shift within months or even weeks.” Stock said the report will document Mistral’s cyber evaluation methods and results, refusal testing and preview monitoring findings. Mistral also intends to share relevant adversarial testing findings “while safeguarding sensitive security information,” he said. He did not give a publication date. ENISA, the EU’s cybersecurity agency, said in a statement published with Mistral’s announcement that it is testing the model to identify vulnerabilities, audit code and analyze defensive logs. Under the EU AI Act, models trained with more than 10^25 floating-point operations (FLOPs) are presumed to carry systemic risk, according to the European Commission . Their providers must assess and mitigate those risks, report serious incidents and maintain cybersecurity protections. Mistral’s post does not say whether Large 4 falls into that category or what risk assessment preceded the release. Stock said Mistral is a full signatory of the EU’s General-Purpose AI Code of Practice, including its safety and security chapter, which the Commission accepts as one way to demonstrate compliance. He did not say whether Large 4 has been classified as a systemic-risk model. Mistral released the model under a modified MIT license that permits use, modification, fine-tuning, and commercialization, the company said. Businesses running a model-as-a-service offering need a separate license. For those who would rather not host it, Mistral’s API is priced at $0.70 per million input tokens and $2.10 per million output tokens. For European buyers, sovereignty is “a meaningful differentiator, but it should not outweigh security concerns,” Dai said. Open weights and self-hosting shift responsibility for guardrails, access controls, monitoring and misuse prevention to the operator, he added. “Sovereignty and security therefore need to be evaluated together, not traded against each other,” Dai said. Daftary said enterprises self-hosting Large 4 for code audit or vulnerability triage should run it as a controlled component, not an autonomous agent. That means isolated environments, least-privilege access to code and credentials, sandboxed generated code, and human sign-off before any remediation, she said. “Self-hosting can improve data control and operational continuity, but it also makes the enterprise solely responsible for patching, monitoring, evaluation and misuse prevention,” she said.
