Webpage.title: Sam Altman sympathizes with mathematicians, but says OpenAI’s math onslaught won’t stop
Webpage.body: Altman says OpenAI has spent hundreds of millions on math — and has more discoveries up its sleeve. Altman says OpenAI has spent hundreds of millions on math — and has more discoveries up its sleeve. After months of bombarding mathematicians with a relentless stream of AI-generated results, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says he sympathizes with researchers struggling to make sense of it all. But he has no intention of stopping — and hints there could be much more to come from the company’s stockpile of discoveries. “I think, on net, the world deserves to understand how the universe works,” Altman said during an episode of the Cheeky Pint podcast released Thursday. “But I do have empathy for the method.” His comments mark one of the first times the OpenAI chief has directly acknowledged the company’s impact on mathematicians, following a string of genuinely impressive AI-generated results whose chaotic , poorly communicated rollouts have left researchers bewildered and struggling to keep up, even amid widespread excitement about AI’s potential as a tool for discovery. Altman argued that the public’s right to new scientific knowledge “outweighs” the disruption caused by OpenAI’s releases, though he acknowledged the company needs to improve how it communicates its findings. “I feel unequivocal on this point: Humanity deserves fundamental knowledge, and we should not be sitting on a major fundamental science discovery,” he said. “The world deserves that.” Mathematicians speaking to The Verge have repeatedly criticized OpenAI for how it announces its results, citing inadequate attribution, little context, and insufficient verification. Researchers say this has left them doing the painstaking work of checking and making sense of their findings even as the company presses ahead with more. This month alone, OpenAI has released hundreds of mathematical results , often with little more than brief writeups that researchers have described as poorly written and hard to follow. Yet OpenAI is now facing criticism for doing precisely what Altman says it should not be: sitting on potentially significant findings. Mathematicians and scientists speaking to The Verge this week said they are frustrated by what they see as OpenAI’s gatekeeping of research , following the announcement of three major breakthroughs in mathematics, physics, and computer science. Details for one of the claimed results — involving Yang-Mills theory, the mathematical foundations of modern particle physics — have not been released publicly. OpenAI says it is due to the recommendations of a hand-picked group of experts it consulted on how best to release it. The practice runs directly counter to the advice of a previous group of mathematicians the company consulted , but forms part of what the company says is a new approach to communicating its findings. On the podcast, Altman hints that OpenAI is sitting on many more mathematical discoveries than it has made public, too. Asked whether the company has more than the hundreds of proofs they have already released, Altman replied: “We do. Of course.” Altman also acknowledged that OpenAI’s pursuit of mathematical problems did “get out of control” for a short period of time, but said that was deliberate and necessary to probe the limits of its AI models. He described an internal Slack channel called “Model Name-Hold My Beer,” where employees “were just throwing that at the hardest problems they could” to see how the models would perform. Altman also estimated that OpenAI has spent in the order of hundreds of millions of dollars tackling mathematical problems, including around $10 million — “maybe a little more” — on its Navier-Stokes solution , one of mathematics’s legendary Millennium Prize problems. The spending offers a glimpse of the vast resources AI labs are bringing to bear on scientific problems, raising concerns among researchers that they may be priced out of their own fields . It looks like mathematicians and other researchers hoping for a breather may be out of luck.

Webpage.title: Maine’s data center revolt will decide who controls the Senate
Webpage.body: Tech billionaires are spending big in Maine’s Senate race. As tech billionaires pour record millions into Maine’s high-stakes Senate race, rural voters push back against the resource strain, rising utility costs, and phantom jobs of the AI data center boom.﻿ As tech billionaires pour record millions into Maine’s high-stakes Senate race, rural voters push back against the resource strain, rising utility costs, and phantom jobs of the AI data center boom.﻿ Maine Sen. Susan Collins, a Republican, was midway through defending her record during the final debate of the midterms when an audience member cut her short. “I’m terrified,” a man shouted. “AI data centers are destroying our climate. They are poisoning our water.” Collins brushed off the outburst, tying the man to her Democratic challenger, Troy Jackson. But the fear echoing through the auditorium wasn’t so easily dismissed. Just days before voters head to the polls, the rapid expansion of resource-hungry data centers has exploded into one of Maine’s most volatile campaign issues. Maine drew national headlines in April when the state Legislature passed what would have been the nation’s first statewide moratorium on large data centers — had Gov. Janet Mills not vetoed the bill 10 days later. But the fight hasn’t slowed down, with towns across the state adopting temporary moratoriums or putting the question of data center expansion to voters this November. In a September poll of Mainers by UMass Lowell and YouGov , 76 percent of respondents said they oppose building a data center in their community, with 58 percent strongly opposed. Maine’s hotly contested Senate race is set to be the most expensive Senate race per capita that the US has ever seen, with Democrats spending a projected $81 million and Republicans $114 million . Much of that campaign cash has come from the very industry Mainers and rural voters across the country have been fighting for more than a year. The outcome of the race will help determine which party controls the Senate and help shape federal data center and AI policy, impacting data center construction not just for Maine residents, but for the entire country. Maine and other rural states are becoming prime targets for new data centers. While cities run short on land and power, Maine has abundant cheap land, vacant industrial mills and buildings, and ample access to water, thanks to its numerous rivers and waterways. Recognizing the high stakes, major tech companies and private equity firms tied to data centers and AI have invested millions in the midterms to win over skeptical locals. The issue has sparked fierce local debate, leading towns and cities across the state to enact temporary bans this summer. Molly White , the researcher, writer, and software engineer behind Tech Influence Watch , says that voters are paying a lot of attention to the issue because they connect data centers to rising costs for utilities. As White points out, many Mainers are also already feeling the pinch due to record-high heating oil costs this fall, and “they’re now looking at an election where the question is, is this candidate going to invite a data center to move in next door, and then my electricity prices go up, or the knock-on effects are going to hurt me even more when I’m already in very dire straits?” she said. White launched her site in 2024 to track crypto spending in political races, but has since expanded it to monitor AI and Big Tech investments. White says the playbook that AI and data center backers are using in the midterms is very similar to the one the cryptocurrency industry used in 2024. “There’s a lot going on in this election,” White says, “but I do think it has been a big issue in Maine and across the country, where you’ll go to a political event, you’ll see people asking questions of candidates, and AI keeps coming up. Certainly there’s a lot of questions about the economy, the war, all these different things, but AI is the new one.” “Certainly there’s a lot of questions about the economy, the war, all these different things, but AI is the new one.” Data center developers and their political allies often sell rural Maine communities on long-term job creation — a promise economists say rarely materializes. In reality, economic research indicates that most data centers create virtually no net employment once construction is complete. Historically, Maine’s industry has centered around lumber and timber, shipbuilding, commercial fishing, textiles, and pulp and paper manufacturing. The timber industry contributed around $8.3 billion to Maine’s economy in 2024, but Donald Trump’s tariffs and rising operating costs have hit it hard, resulting in mill closures and layoffs. Mark Brewer , who chairs the political science department at the University of Maine, says Maine’s history complicates the debate. These former mill towns jump at the chance to rebuild their local tax bases and infrastructure, but past boom-and-bust cycles make residents cautious. “Maine has a long history of extractive industries providing jobs,” Brewer says, which allowed Mainers to tolerate these industries despite the state’s environmental focus. With data centers thus far, he says, “the jobs part of it’s not there. It’s one thing to put up with a paper mill that’s employing three shifts of 1,000 workers, right? Data centers aren’t doing that.” For many rural Mainers, the question is not only whether a data center will bring jobs back, but whether to trust the companies promising them or the government helping make the deal, said Nicholas Jacobs , the director of the Public Policy Lab at Colby College in Maine. These residents say they’re concerned about the opaque ownership of these data centers, limited long-term employment, and the risk of wealth being extracted from rural communities. Tech and AI interests see an ally in Susan Collins, the 73-year-old Republican chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee. Like most congressional Republicans, she has largely supported data centers and AI, though she has said she believes data centers should be evaluated on an individual basis . Collins has even used her position as head of the Appropriations Committee to secure $6.2 million in federal funding for a high-performance computing hub data center in central Maine, which is designed to bolster localized AI and biotech research. Her stance has brought in a tremendous amount of campaign donations from Big Tech, AI, and data center donors for her reelection bid. Collins’ individual donors include Alex Karp, the cofounder and CEO of Palantir; Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz of VC firm Andreessen Horowitz, which heavily backs data centers; and others from Google, Meta, and Microsoft. According to White’s donation tracker , Collins has received $325,644 from AI and crypto donors. Data centers aren’t doing that.” Super PACs like the Republican Senate Leadership Fund dumped nearly $42 million into ads across Maine. Elon Musk gave $158 million to the Senate Leadership Fund this summer , and has spent around $450 million of his own money to support Republicans in the midterms . Musk’s America PAC has spent around $2.1 million in Maine . Pine Tree Results PAC, to which Collins and her husband have personal ties, put $29.1 million into the race to support her. Webpage.title: From synthetic enterprise data evaluations to real Microsoft Copilot AI confidence
Webpage.body: Evaluating Microsoft Copilot at enterprise scale requires test data that captures the full complexity of real organizations, yet real enterprise data contains sensitive information that cannot be used for evaluation under any circumstances. Every day, millions of knowledge workers around the world rely on Microsoft Copilot to draft documents, summarize meetings, surface relevant information, and accelerate productivity. Behind the scenes, this is powered by a network of AI systems, and ensuring they work as intended requires a thoughtful approach to evaluation. At Microsoft, we know that high performance doesn’t come from guesswork. It comes from testing, measuring, and iterating constantly. Healthcare organizations are constantly synthesizing safety signals from across teams so that they can make faster, better decisions that directly influence patient outcomes and regulatory confidence. They may ask Copilot to summarize a meeting and extract action items for their teams. Within seconds, Copilot delivers a structured summary citing specific discussion points from the transcript. But how do we ensure this response is accurate, complete, and properly grounded in the meeting content? This is where our evaluation system comes in. We’ve developed a structured evaluation strategy called Industry Evaluation Data Generation Platform , which includes industry specific evaluation datasets designed to test AI systems against realistic enterprise scenarios, grounded in three core pillars: Together, these pillars help us answer two fundamental questions: Is Microsoft Copilot actually doing what our users need it to do, and can we prove it without ever touching their data ? In this blog post, we’ll walk through our evaluation system and processes, from synthetic environment generation to automated query pipelines, and how it all comes together to establish the first standardized evaluation baseline for Microsoft Copilot. Evaluating enterprise AI requires test data that captures the full complexity of real organizations: reporting structures, project histories, communication patterns, and domain specific workflows. But real enterprise data contains sensitive information that cannot be used for evaluation under any circumstances. This is the central tension we set out to resolve. Rather than relying on small, manually curated test fixtures, we generate full scale synthetic environments : simulated enterprise workspaces, each with realistic organizational structures, communication histories, and work artifacts. In Microsoft terminology, each of these simulated workspaces is called a “tenant”. A tenant is an isolated organizational environment with its own users, data, and configurations. These environments are scalable baselines that teams and organizations can build off of however they want. They are designed to exhibit the same structural and behavioral properties that make enterprise AI evaluation meaningful. To ensure our synthetic environments are realistic, we grounded them in publicly available real world data sources. Importantly, these synthetic environments are not static snapshots. They simulate dynamic, time-evolving organizations with meeting histories, project timelines, email threads that develop over weeks, and organizational changes that unfold naturally. This temporal dimension is essential because a large class of Copilot queries are inherently time aware. Questions like “What did the team decide last Thursday?” or “What’s changed since the last quarterly review?” only produce meaningful evaluations if the underlying data has a genuine temporal structure. We generated three synthetic environments across multiple industries, each with distinct characteristics that mirror real world usage: This industry specificity ensures that our evaluation queries test Copilot against the kinds of questions real users in those domains actually ask, rather than relying on generic test cases that may not surface domain specific failure modes. While synthetic environments provide the substrate for evaluation, they face a key limitation: we still need realistic evaluation queries. These are the questions that test whether Copilot can surface the right information, synthesize it correctly, and present it helpfully. Manually writing thousands of grounded, industry specific queries is prohibitively expensive and slow. That’s where our automated pipeline comes in. We built an automated pipeline that turns simple, generic query ideas into realistic, industry-specific questions for Copilot. It starts with a large library of common workplace tasks, narrows them down to what’s relevant for a given industry, and adapts them using domain-specific language and context. The system then uses AI to generate queries grounded in the synthetic environment’s data, rewrites them to sound more natural and human, and validates each one for accuracy and uniqueness. The result is a rich set of high-quality, lifelike queries that enable scalable and reliable evaluation of Copilot across real-world scenarios. Of course, generating synthetic data is only part of the challenge. We also need to ensure the data is good enough to produce meaningful evaluations. We assess synthetic environment quality using our internal semantic evaluation framework which measures quality across three dimensions: While our synthetic environments and query pipelines provide the methodology, they face several practical limitations without proper automation, including: This automation reduced evaluation dataset creation from a multi-day manual process to automated runs. We estimate savings of approximately $100,000 per evaluation dataset and $300,000 in total project savings. But the more important outcome is that any team can now regenerate an evaluation dataset from the same configuration and get identical results. Join us for a continuous exchange of ideas about research in the era of general AI. Watch the latest episodes on demand. Enterprise grade evaluation demands more than good methodology. It requires a privacy posture that allows teams to move fast without compromising user trust. A non-negotiable design principle of our industry evaluation datasets is that no real customer data is used at any stage of the pipeline . Every element, from organizational structures to email content to meeting transcripts, is synthetically generated, with no customer data inputs. Because the data is both fully synthetic and safety-screened, teams can share and reuse it widely without introducing reputational, compliance, or Responsible AI risk. Our safeguards include privacy preserving aggregation techniques where real-world statistical distributions are referenced, expert legal review and approval of all public data sources, and clear data provenance and lineage tracking throughout the pipeline. This means teams across Microsoft can use these evaluation datasets freely for experimentation, benchmarking, and regression testing without privacy review overhead or data handling restrictions that would otherwise slow down iteration. The privacy design is not a constraint on the system. It is what makes broad adoption possible. Since starting this project, we have observed significant improvements across multiple dimensions. On synthetic data quality , our internal scoring system showed significant quality gains in the structural, contextual, and statistical fidelity of the generated data. Across our composite quality metric (which measures how closely synthetic data mirrors the complexity and patterns of real enterprise environments), scores improved 39% compared to our initial generation approach. Some industry-specific environments reached quality scores above 0.9 out of 1.0, demonstrating that domain focused generation produces highly realistic evaluation environments. Webpage.title: Microsoft Research Focus – Edition #97
Webpage.body: Host Sowbhagya Suresh shares some of the latest news and cutting-edge research from across Microsoft—from understanding the challenges facing coding agents to uncovering how people use AI at work and improving extended-range weather forecasting. You may already be familiar with the Research Focus newsletter (opens in new tab) on LinkedIn. Now, you can catch up on highlights from across the research community at Microsoft on our social channels, YouTube, and major podcast platforms, too. In this edition of Microsoft Research Focus , host Sowbhagya Suresh shares some of the latest news and cutting-edge research from across Microsoft—from understanding the challenges facing coding agents to uncovering how people use AI at work and improving extended-range weather forecasting. Catch up on the ideas, tools, and discoveries researchers are exploring today and get a quick look at what’s coming next. SOWBHAGYA SURESH: Hi, I’m Sowbhagya Suresh. Welcome to Microsoft Research Focus . You’ve probably read our newsletter. And now you can get highlights from across the research community at Microsoft here, on YouTube, and major podcast platforms. Whether you read, watch, or listen to it, Research Focus is your source for research news at Microsoft. Coming up in this edition: what everyday AI use reveals about the way we work; how a new AI model could help scientists better understand proteins; a new approach to improving weather forecasts weeks in advance; and more. So here’s what’s new. More and more, AI agents are handling tasks that are complex. Tasks that require multiple steps, decisions, and interactions with external tools. But how can we count on AI agents to do the work if their ability to adjust when things go wrong may require a lot of resources with no guarantees of a better result? A new self-improving framework called ForkPilot learns when it’s worth revisiting earlier decisions to find a different approach and adapts its strategy based on new outcomes. Tested across six benchmarks and leading AI models, ForkPilot measures up to the best existing methods while reducing AI processing demands by up to 59%. These results suggest that AI agents can solve complex problems more reliably and efficiently, making them more practical and cost-effective to deploy at scale. Coding agents execute user queries by reasoning about, editing, and running code. Understanding why these agents fail is critical if we want to build more capable and reliable coding agents. Unfortunately, existing benchmarks often make it difficult to identify which factors contribute to success or failure. CABRA is a framework for generating coding challenges from scratch. It lets researchers increase complexity in a controlled way and pinpoints the skills that are most difficult for agents. Across thousands of generated challenges, the researchers found that agents often overcame coding problems by using tools. Yet the agents still struggled when they needed to understand unfamiliar codebases. The findings suggest that understanding existing code, rather than modifying it, remains one of the biggest obstacles to developing more effective coding agents. Computer-use agents are AI systems that are designed to complete tasks that require clicking and typing. They can fill in forms, process requests, and navigate websites. To do this effectively, they need to learn the procedures that people use to get work done. User activity logs can offer a way to capture this knowledge. But activity logs typically don’t record the intent behind each action and often combine tasks. The new framework TeleTune learns reusable skills and workflows from these logs. It also infers the task goals associated with the sequences of actions. In evaluations across software and browser tasks, TeleTune outperformed existing approaches. By learning from existing activity, TeleTune offers a scalable way to help AI agents adapt to unfamiliar software and carry out complex, multi-step workflows Workers across industries may appear to be using AI in surprisingly similar ways, but a closer look reveals a different story. Microsoft researchers analyzed aggregated Copilot Chat activity across a broad range of customer categories and found that editing documents led all classified activities, accounting for more than 20 percent. But when researchers set aside the 20 most common activities, differences between customer categories became substantially more pronounced. The most common uses of AI may be hiding important differences in how organizations use it for more specialized work. For business leaders, the takeaway is clear: don’t assume you have the same AI needs as others in your industry. Finding the right opportunities means looking beyond usage statistics to understand what employees actually do, how they work, and what outcomes matter most. A new study shows how Shiksha Copilot—a human-in-the-loop AI tool—could transform teacher workflows in Global South classrooms. The study in low-resource schools in India found the tool reduced the time teachers spent on bilingual lesson planning and bureaucracy. That gave them more time to craft more engaging classroom activities. More than a thousand teachers participated, and many reported reduced stress levels and a positive impression of how AI can help them. These teachers actively engaged with Shiksha Copilot, using their professional expertise to adapt and repurpose materials to suit their own classrooms. Ten-day weather forecasts have become remarkably dependable. But what about the weeks that follow? The two-to-six-week window remains a major challenge for forecasting models, which is a problem. That’s when a wide range of critical decisions get made related to farming, managing wildfires, and preparing for extreme weather. A new machine-learning framework called Probabilistic Bias Correction, or PBC , is helping close that gap. PBC learns from a weather model’s past mistakes and helps correct them. PBC took top honors in a global competition focused on improving extended-range forecasting. It’s also being deployed in Kenya, where it’s helping improve critical monsoon forecasts for farmers. This development could help make weather predictions more useful across a broad range of applications. BioEmu2, a new foundation model for understanding biomolecular structure, dynamics, and function, is now available in public preview. Developed by the Microsoft Research AI for Science team, BioEmu2 builds on Biomolecular Emulator, a deep-learning model designed to help scientists better understand how proteins work. That understanding could have important implications for medicine. By learning more about how proteins function, scientists could move closer to developing more effective medications that enhance beneficial protein activity or prevent proteins from causing harm. From more capable AI agents to better weather forecasting, these are just a few of the developments researchers are exploring at Microsoft. Want to learn more and stay connected? Explore the latest research, discover the people behind it, and keep tabs on the ideas shaping what’s next by following Microsoft Research on major social platforms. I’m Sowbhagya Suresh. Thanks so much for tuning in. We’ll see you in the next Microsoft Research Focus.

Webpage.title: Mistral releases weights for its trillion-parameter AI model, targeting cybersecurity | TechCrunch
Webpage.body: Mistral says its new model can afford organizations a kind of control over its cyber defenses that closed models can't. French AI company Mistral has released the weights for its trillion-parameter open source AI model Mistral Large 4 (ML4), allowing businesses and governments to download and deploy the system themselves. Nicknamed “Le Chonk,” the model was first introduced earlier this month . The release comes as competition between open-weight AI developers like Mistral and closed-model providers like OpenAI and Anthropic heats up, with the former arguing that businesses and governments shouldn’t have to rely on outside AI companies for access to advanced capabilities. That argument may hold more weight in cybersecurity, where organizations want more control over their data and systems. Or, as Mistral’s CEO, Arthur Mensch, explained, AI should “be a tool for empowerment, not dominance.” With Chonk, Mistral doubles down on that position, arguing that it’s able to achieve “state-of-the-art performance” at a “fraction of the compute and capital committed by closed labs.” The release of the model’s weights — the numerical training that animates the system — ensures that other companies and government agencies will now be able to deploy ML4 for their own purposes. Mistral says that its model is comparable in terms of performance with a Chinese open-weight competitor, GLM-5.3, which was previously considered one of the best open-weight models in the world — particularly when it comes to cyber work. However, Mistral’s model uses 47 percent fewer tokens per task, making it significantly more economical than GLM-5.3. The company also claims that the model outranks all other open models when it comes to agentic coding tasks on Artificial Analysis’ Coding Agent Index, an AI benchmarking site. “Amid growing cyber threats, ML4 brings state-of-the-art sovereign cyber defense capabilities to enterprises and governments globally,” the company said Thursday. “Enterprise and public sector institutions can now download, deploy, and own frontier AI to detect, analyze, and respond to threats across code and IT infrastructure.” The weights for ML4 are being made available on Hugging Face and via its API. Pierre Stock, Vice President of Science at Mistral, told TechCrunch that the release of the model’s weights meant that organizations will have more control over how they use AI to defend themselves. “Concretely, it means that, for instance, as a business company or as a government, you’re able to have access to frontier intelligence to defend yourselves against cyberattacks. Access that can’t be cut off by definition because the model is open-weighted,” he said. Stock added that the model could be used to “identify, coordinate, and respond in real time to major security incidents, and that the open sourcing means that companies can deploy this model on-prem in their own ecosystem. While advances in AI cybersecurity are helping security professionals to find bugs at a much higher rate than before, Stock continued, he believes it’s important for companies to “provide [this same] capability to everyone…as soon as possible to ramp up and to strengthen the ecosystem,” given that “some malicious actors might try to actually leverage their own technology to attack.” Separately, Stock addressed concerns about recent incidents involving rogue AI agents, acknowledging the risks but cautioning against overreacting. “We don’t want to fearmonger people. We think it’s a problem that is solvable. It’s a hard problem to have good security,” he said. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . Webpage.title: SpaceX loses bid to toss NAACP lawsuit over Memphis data center air pollution
Webpage.body: SpaceX's AI division, SpaceXAI, lost its bid to dismiss an NAACP lawsuit, which is proceeding in federal court in Mississippi, according to a judge's opinion released late Friday. The lawsuit claims that the AI division of CEO Elon Musk's aerospace and defense tech conglomerate violated the Clean Air Act with its use of gas-fired combustion turbines to power its massive AI data centers in Greater Memphis. The Colossus data centers and a power plant that SpaceXAI is also building in Southaven, Mississippi, have faced community backlash for years. The Southern Environmental Law Center and Earthjustice filed the suit on behalf of the NAACP in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Mississippi in April 2026. The suit alleges that between August and December 2025, xAI and its subsidiary MZX Tech, installed and operated 27 gas turbines in Southaven, Mississippi, "without an air permit or regard for the health and safety of people living nearby." (SpaceXAI is owned and operated by SpaceX, which has rebranded it as SpaceXAI or SpaceXSI.) The turbines emit smog-forming pollutants and particulate matter that can increase health risks and cause an unpleasant odor, among other unwanted impacts, according to the suit. Lawyers for SpaceXAI argued in their motion to dismiss, filed in June, that the NAACP suit should be tossed because the company's use of the turbines, which it characterized as "mobile," was exempt from permitting requirements. They also argued that NAACP didn't have a right to sue under the federal Clean Air Act, and suits by such community groups were unconstitutional. The judge presiding over the case rejected those arguments, writing: "Because the plaintiffs have statutory standing under the Clean Air Act, because the combustion turbines are not 'mobile sources' under Mississippi's SIP, and because the citizen suit provision does not violate Article II of the Constitution or the private nondelegation doctrine, the plaintiffs' claims will proceed." The decision comes about two weeks after the same court rejected a Department of Justice's request to end the case against Musk's company. SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Intel shares plummeted 29% on Friday, their worst day since the 1970s, after the chipmaker issued weaker-than-expected guidance due to a plant shutdown in Israel and ongoing softness in the PC market. It's a major setback for CEO Lip-Bu Tan, who was hired in March 2025, and has since been on a campaign to revive the company after it missed out on the early years of the artificial intelligence boom. Intel's plunge is also a big hit to the Trump administration, which led the U.S. government into taking a 10% stake in the company over a year ago. While it's still a profitable investment, the value of those holdings dropped by about $12 billion on Friday. Nvidia also took a big stake in Intel, and its stock dropped by about $6 billion in value. Heading into Thursday's earnings report, Intel shares were up about 150% this year, buoyed by demand for central processors, which are becoming critical to agentic AI workloads. Analysts at D.A. Davidson downgraded the stock to neutral from buy on Friday in a report titled, "Not fixed yet." "We understand the PC market is being impacted at the industry level," the analysts wrote. "However it is hard to justify the current multiple when weakness is so significant." Amazon shares also sold off on Friday, slipping 1.4%, after the company reported a third-quarter miss on the top and bottom line while maintaining its capital expenditure forecast for 2026 of $220 billion. Amazon also reported negative free cash flow for the second consecutive quarter, and a big increase from the previous period. The Nasdaq Composite slid 2.9%, capping off a week of rough tech earnings. Alphabet on Thursday suffered its worst day on record, plunging more than 12%. The stock fell again on Friday. Other semiconductor names also notched declines. Chip giant Nvidia fell 4%, while Broadcom dropped more than 5% and mobile chipmaker Qualcomm tumbled 11%. Investors are growing nervous about the massive AI spending from the tech giants and whether their investments will pay off. "I don't think this is a moment of reckoning but I think it's a moment where investors should take a long thought about how positioning across the space still remains crowded even though the fundamentals are strong," Matt Orton, chief market strategist at Raymond James, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Friday. For Intel, the disappointing forecast reflects a PC market that's getting hammered due to soaring costs for memory and other components. Global PC shipments declined 4% in the second quarter from a year earlier, according to Counterpoint Research . Intel said it expects adjusted earnings per share of 25 cents this quarter on revenue between $15 billion and $16 billion. Analysts were expecting revenue of $17.1 billion and EPS of 43 cents, according to LSEG. "We see the PC slowdown continuing at least through the first half of next year," Intel finance chief David Zinsner, said in the release. "We will continue making disciplined investments in capacity and working capital to increase supply and support future growth." The guidance also accounts for the effects of an explosion at a fab in Israel that killed two workers and seriously injured a third earlier this month. The incident will cost the company about $600 million in lost revenue over two quarters, Zinsner said. Tan said the explosion, which he called an "unfortunate and tragic accident," caused an "extended shutdown" at the plant, impacting shipments of 10-nanometer chips. Key to Tan's turnaround effort is Intel's foundry business, which has struggled to find its footing. Intel is the only U.S.-based manufacturer of advanced logic chips, and is now in high-volume production of its most advanced 18A chip out of its new fab in Arizona, providing an alternative to Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co . Its next Arizona fab is expected to begin operations by the end of 2028. "We're going to have a couple of customers ready to announce the next two quarters," Tan said on the call, adding that Intel is making "tremendous progress" on its coming 14A chips.

Webpage.title: Theranos whistleblower Tyler Shultz on Elizabeth Holmes film
Webpage.body: Tyler Shultz reacts to Nathan Fielder’s Elizabeth Holmes film Tyler Shultz knows a thing or two about fraud. He says the AI money boom is the perfect setup for the next Theranos. Has everyone fallen under Elizabeth Holmes’ spell again? Nathan Fielder’s sort-of documentary “You Can See Everything” has reignited interest in the story of the Theranos fraudster — and this time around, people seem to find her sympathetic. So we asked someone who has spent nearly half his life thinking about Holmes to separate fact from fiction. Tyler Shultz met Holmes at Stanford, worked under her at Theranos, and helped expose the company’s seemingly miraculous blood-testing technology as a sham. In his first longform interview since the release of “You Can See Everything,” Shultz reckons with being a high-profile whistleblower and shares his reaction to a film that treats its subject with deliberate ambiguity. He thinks it’s a mistake to believe Holmes — an argument he laid out in the science and healthcare publication Stat (opens in new tab) after the film’s release. He sees her as a practiced manipulator obsessed with her public image and points to her comeback, achieved from prison: a People cover, a starring turn in one of the most talked-about films of the year, and according to Shultz, a hand in her partner Billy Evans’ new blood-testing startup. Holmes, Shultz believes, is still playing her audience. “I feel like the only reason we’re talking about Elizabeth Holmes right now is because she wants us to be talking about Elizabeth Holmes right now,” Shultz told guest host Theo Baker on this week’s “PST.” Shultz is confident Holmes won’t be the last fraudster Silicon Valley has to contend with. The conditions that enabled her to raise hundreds of millions of dollars without adequate scrutiny are more prevalent than ever, Shultz believes, because AI is uniquely hard to vet and because we’re living in a “world that cares less about the truth.” “It’s really hard to tell the difference between something truly unique versus a ChatGPT wrapper,” he said. “If you want to deceive people, I think this is a great opportunity to go deceive people.”

Webpage.title: Google Also Adopts New AI Training Control
Webpage.body: Google is adopting new AI training controls, under consideration by the IETF, that should simplify and streamline AI training controls for publishers and site owners. Google also announced , like Bing , OpenAI and Anthropic , that it plans to voluntarily adopt a proposal under consideration at IETF , the global internet standard-setting body, that would create a simple, streamlined AI training control for web publishers and creators. Google said, "This will help websites express their AI training preferences across multiple AI providers in a single step and is based on work from the AIPREF working group at the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF)." This new, work-in-progress control will give websites and publishers a new way to communicate their AI training preferences across multiple AI providers. This lets them invoke their preferences in a single step in robots.txt, instead of listing each one individually. Google told me "moving forward with this initiative alongside peer AI providers as part of a shared commitment to foster an open, creator-first web ecosystem, and following feedback from publishers, civil society and regulators calling for an easier way for websites to express their AI training preferences." Instead of managing separate instructions for every AI developer, website owners will be able to use a shared 'policy token' within robots.txt to set broad preferences across participating AI providers. Keep in mind, Google also has the Search Console opt out method for Search generative AI. Google also updated its common crawlers page to mention future AI training control support. Google added a note that says: Existing company-specific controls will continue to function alongside this new joint signal. So website owners can easily express a broad choice using the industry signal, while also tailoring their instructions to individual AI developers like Google through controls such as Google-Extended. Websites that specifically allow Google-Extended are eligible to appear in responses and receive clicks via grounding in Gemini Apps. The new mechanism brings website owners the benefit of the AI training definition developed at the IETF while multistakeholder discussions continue on the rest of the AIPREF vocabulary. As more industry players adopt this mechanism, it gives website owners early and expanding access to the preference signal. This draft proposal reflects feedback from publishers, civil society groups, regulators and other stakeholders that have called for industry-wide controls on AI training. Support for this proposal across major AI providers will enable a future standard that is cross-industry, robust, and durable. This proposal is consistent with the EU Code of Practice for General Purpose AI (GPAI) Model Providers under the EU AI Act that recognizes robots.txt as a primary method for web publishers to express machine-readable preferences. We'll continue to work with these stakeholders to refine and standardize this through the IETF working group. We aim to support this new control along with other AI providers in 2027, and will provide updates on our progress. This may be helpful from Vanessa Fox in better understanding this change. I also updated my tool to check for the new user-agent. You can read the announcements here: https://t.co/FdQELlzled & https://t.co/jvnON5wTvj & https://t.co/lDUUXvBQHx & https://t.co/H1m7mPEpvU Also, it seems like the IETF didn't just have these talks with Google, Microsoft, OpenAI and Anthropic, but also both large and small publishers to chime in: @rustybrick @gaganghotra_ fyi, Barry, i've been spending the last year deeply participating in this group. you'll notice my name at the bottom in the acknowledgments. if you need help understanding, dm (also, fyi, it's not actually done at the ietf level -- and some significant areas of dispute remain) this was our latest (short) interim. https://t.co/Sd8qKgMBJz here's one (of many) videos from our 3 day meeting in london: https://t.co/oRyBooGaOz ive been one of the more vocal participants. you'll notice at the end of the latest interim recording, and also in my latest emails, that i'm still quite unhappy about one thing in the current draft (it basically exempts the preferences from applying to anything a user does, which hurts artists and creators getting hammered by AI spam copycats). but generally the process has been productive, and it's not over yet. One note - they didn’t actually invite me or anyone else. They don’t do invites. IETF is a public and transparent group anyone can participate in. Its mostly gated by the fact that it takes a lot of time and effort to meaningfully contribute. I just found out about it and chose to invest the 100s of hours and thousands of $ in travel costs to participate this past year. Webpage.title: We’ve received our first response from the Project Suncatcher prototype satellite.
Webpage.body: On October 1, we launched our prototype satellite for Project Suncatcher. The launch marked the first step in our long-term research moonshot to explore powering AI compute in space. Since then, we've spent the last few weeks completing our commissioning checklist, which included powering up the host and TPU trays and successfully running early machine learning tests. This week, we reached our "Hello World" milestone: the first-ever AI response from a data center class TPU in orbit. During a ground-station pass, we uplinked our first prompt to our onboard Gemma 4 open model, asking it to generate a haiku about being in space. As the satellite passed by Svalbard, Norway, the downlinked poem confirmed success: Blue marble below Data streams in silent grace Starlight feeds my core. ✨ Following this initial output, we tested space-themed limericks and telemetry prompts reporting the technical status of the payload systems. Next, we will continue with a series of tests to evaluate how TPUs perform under thermal stress and radiation exposure in orbit. Verifying our TPUs can reliably execute workloads in space paves the way for our next milestone of twin interconnected satellites in 2027. Our chips have officially earned their space wings — an important achievement on the long road ahead for this cosmic moonshot.
